141. The provision of Article 7 of the constitution has been identified in judicial pronouncement as 'pole star' of our Constitution which has to be taken into consideration, in order to examine as to whether the parliament, being the creative of the constitution, enjoys omnipotence in enacting any law in their wisdom. The said article reads as follows;

Constitution of Bangladesh

Article 7:

(১) প্রজাতন্ত্রের সকল ক্ষমতার মালিক জনগণ এবং জনগণের পক্ষে সেই ক্ষমতার প্রয়োগ কেবল এই সংবিধানের অধীন ও কর্তৃত্বে কার্যাকর হইবে।

(২)জনগণের অভিপ্রায়ের পরম অভিব্যক্তিরূপে এই সংবিধান প্রজাতন্ত্রের সর্বোচ্চ আইন এবং অন্য কোন আইন যদি এই সংবিধানের সহিত অসামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণ, ততখানি বাতিল হইবে।

Article 7: Supremacy of the Constitution

(1)	All powers in the Republic belong to the people, and their exercise on behalf of the people shall be effected only under and by the authority of, this Constitution.

(2)	this Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency be void.]

142. The supreme law of our country has declared the supremacy of the people for exercising power of the republic and such exercise was made subject to the provisions of the constitution. This has restricted the pertinent to exceed its power beyond the provisions of the constitution. The parliament is also restricted in its legislative power under the provision of Article 26 (2) of the Constitution and the same also required to be taken into consideration in order to ascertain whether the parliament hai omnipotence in enacting laws.

143. Undoubtedly the parliament has been vested with the legislative power. But that power has to be exercised within the four corners of the Constitution. The provision of article 7 and 26 of the Constitution substantially restricted such legislative power and, as such, when such legislative power is being exercised, the parliament has to take note of it.

144. The provisions of article 65 of the constitution made the parliament sovereign, not as omnipotent, but within the bounds of the constitution and the provisions of article 7(2) and 26(1) and (2) of the Constitution made the parliament not that omnipotent to enact any law as per its wisdom and desire. It can enact law, subject to the provision of the constitution. If it enacts any law that contradicts any provision of the constitution, then that part of the law will be void as has been provided under article 7(2) read with article 26 (1)(2) of the constitution.

<u>145. Therefore, this bench finds that provision of section 16CCC of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 as incorporated in the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 through the provision of section 15 of the Finance Act 2011 being contradictory, inconsistent and contrary to the aim and object of the said statute and violative of the provision of article 31 and 7(2) and 26 (1)(2) of the Constitution, is a piece of legislation which the parliament is not authorized to enact and thereby liable to be declared ultra vices of the constitution.</u>

146. Now turning to the 3rd issue as to discriminatory effect of the impugned section 16CCC this bench examined the provision of article 27 of the Constitution which deal with such issue. The provision of article 27 of the Constitution runs as follows;

বাংলাদেশ সংবিধান

অনুচ্ছেদ ২৭: আইনের দৃষ্টিতে সমতা-

সকল নাগরিক আইনের দৃষ্টিতে সমান এবং আইনের সমান আশ্রয়লাভের অধিকারী।

All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law].

147. Equality before law has been a long disputed issue resolved in many previous cases. out of which the referred case of Hayes Maier Appliances Co. Ltd vs IRD; reported in 58 DLR 5 may be profitably examined.

148. In that case his-lordship Mr Justice Syed Amirul Islam while dealing with the issue examined the various decisions of the home and the Indian Jurisdiction and ultimately held that.

"In 41 DLR (AD) 30, it has been held that the term protection of equal law is used to mean that all-persons or things are not equal in all cases and that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. Equal protection is the guarantee that similar people will be dealt with in a similar way. The legislature which proceeding to make law with certain object in view has power to make classification on reasonable basis. To stand that test of `equality, a classification, besides being based on intelligent differentia, must have reasonable nexus with the object the legislation intends to achieve by making the classification. What is of fundamental importance in law making is that while making a classification the legislature shall not act arbitrarily but make selection on rational basis.

A review of the aforesaid decision shows that it is now well settled while Article 27 forbids class legislation it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification two conditions must be fulfilled, namely, (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and (ii) that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. The classification may be founded on different basis, namely, geographical or according to objects or occupations or the like. What is necessary is that there must be a nexus between the basis of classification and the object of the Act under consideration. It is also well established that Article 27 condemns discrimination not only by a substantive law but also by a law of procedure.

<u>149. The impugned provision of section 16CCC only imposed minimum tax liability upon two of the three classes of assessee standing on the same footing conducting a similar and identical business the individual tax payer will be relieved from paying the minimum tax which is hit by the principle as enunciated in the referred case.</u>

150. Similar provision of minimum tax, prevailing in other countries as referred by the learned Additional Attorney-General cannot be taken into consideration in order to treat the constitutionality of a provision of law which is violative of our constitution and, as such, labour and pain exercised by the learned Additional Attorney-General Mr Murad-E- Reza in this respect falls flat.

151. The learned Additional Attorney-General perhaps failed to recollect the admission

of the Honourable Finance Advisor Dr. AB Mirza Muhammad Azizul Islam as to the illegality of the similar provision embodied in the repealed section 16CC of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 for which nothing has been heard on that issue of admission from the learned Additional Attorney-General.

152. This bench has meticulously examined the other decisions, as referred to by the learned Additional Attorney-General and found that are not being applicable to the issue of these writ petitions, has no manner of application to the issue in front of this court.

153. Under the reasoning and discussion as above this court finds merit in these rules Nisi, which are required to be made absolute.

154. In the result, these rules Nisi are made absolute.

155. The provision of section 16CCC of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 as has been incorporated in the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 through section 15 of the Finance Act 2011 is hereby declared ultra vices to the constitution having been enacted without any lawful authority having no legal implication.

156. However, there shall be no order as to costs. The order of stay against the operation of the said impugned provision of section 16CCC of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 is hereby made absolute.

Md Ashfaqul Islam J: I regret that I could not subscribe to the .views expressed in the judgment of my learned brother AFM Abdur Rahman, J. while striking down section 16CCC of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. The reasons for my disagreement are as under:

158. The background leading to the Rules featured in all the writ petitions has been craftily outlined by His Lordship which I 'need not require to revisit for expounding my own reasoning’s. I would quote only those of the relevant laws and related aspects as and when required.

159. The gravamen of the petitioners' grievances in all the petitions is the insertion of section 16CCC in Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 (hereinafter referred to as Ordinance) by the Finance Act 201.1 on the plea of the same being violative of the object, spirit, purport and scheme of the Ordinance so to say, law of income tax as a whole and also the fundamental right of the petitioners enshrined in the Constitution. Section 16CCC begins with a non-obstante clause that overriding whatever contained in the Ordinance 1984 a minimum tax @ Zero Point Three Zero percent (0.30%) shall be charged upon every firm having "gross receipts" of more than Taka 50,00,000 lakh (restricted implication) or every company irrespective of profit and loss in an assessment year.

160. The meaning of 'gross receipts' has been construed by an explanation to the law itself.

161. Now the issue that to be addressed with reference to the context of all the petitions is whether under the given situation and upon critical appraisal of the different laws in the Ordinance and divergent submissions from the Bar conjunct with the Constitutional mandate and its bearing on the issue, together with the interpretation of fiscal Statute, Section 16CCC of the Ordinance would sustain in the manner as it has found place in the Ordinance as a valid piece of enactment.

162. For better understanding and appreciating the subject I would like to view it from a totally different perspective. When any legislation is read as it is, a question pertinently comes into mind why is that legislation for. In other words, what is law, and why the law is. What is law, can be sensed at a glance on a mere reading of it but why the law is meant for can only be obviated from the intention of the legislature behind the enactment of a particular law. The intention has to be gathered from the attending circumstances, some probable exigencies and far reaching consequences which may not be crystallized merely upon plain reading of bare provisions of the Ordinance.

163. Saying so much I would now digress to assess the vires of law under challenge on numerous counts which his Lordship has already addressed at length. One of the pivotal arguments from the bar that has been taken into consideration by my brother Rahman, J is that when by Finance Act 2008 section 16CC of the ordinance was omitted, in the budget speech of 2008-2009 the then Finance Minister Advisor Dr. A.B. Mirza Mohammad Azizul Islam had admitted that the provisions of Section 16CC of the Ordinance was inconsistent with the provisions of Ordinance 1984 and, as such, the same was required to be omitted from the Statute. To assess this aspect it would be worthwhile to view it in the light of the observations made by the Supreme Court of India in the case of K? Varghese vs CIT 131 ITR 397 (SC):

"It is true that speeches made by the member of the Legislature on the floor of the House when a Bill for enacting a statutory provision is being debated are  inadmissible  for the purpose of interpreting the statutory provision but the speech made by mover of the Bill explaining the reason for the introduction of the Bill can certainly be referred to for the purpose of ascertaining the mischief 'sought to be remedied by the legislation and the object and the purpose for which the .legislation was enacted. This is in accordance with the recent trend in juristic thought not only in western countries but also in India that interpretation of Statute being an exercise in the ascertainment of meaning: everything, which is logically relevant, should be admissible."

164. Upon overall analysis of the reasons for introduction of section 16CCC in the Ordinance one aspect comes out clear that intention of legislature to enact the same was mainly for the reason that some unscrupulous firm and company were willfully trying to avoid payment of tax always contending that they are running at a loss and for that reason the legislature in its wisdom thought it proper to insert the section as it has been done in several countries throughout the World. The concept of charging minimum tax by now has earned status of a beneficial Statute. In case of a beneficial Statute its provisions cannot be interpreted so as to bring about a result contrary to the object of the legislation. An interpretation likely to advance the remedy must be adopted in case of Statute, which confer benefit on individual or any class of person. The perception should be in the context of the nation as a whole.

165. It is well settled that the language employed in fiscal law has to be strictly construed and be given its plain and natural meaning and in such Statute one has to look merely as what is said therein and there is no room for any intendment. Nothing is to be read in and nothing is to be implied. One can look fairly at the language used. CIT vs Zeenat Textile Mills Ltd. 6 BTD 85 (AD).

166. While interpreting section 45A of the Income Tax Ordinance 1922 to be unambiguous, CJ Hamoodur Rahman (as he then was), in Md Ismail vs State 21 DLR (SC) 161, expressed in the following words

"The purpose of construction or interpretation of statutory provision is no doubt to ascertain the true intention of the Legislature, yet that intention has, of necessity, to be gathered from the words used by the Legislature itself. If those words are so clear and unmistakable that they cannot be given any meaning other than that which they carry in their ordinary grammatical sense, then the Courts are not concerned with the consequences of the interpretation, however, drastic or inconvenient the result, for, the function of the Courts is interpretation not  legislation."

167. In the case of M/s Gulistan Cinema Co. 28 DLR 16 (AD) it was held that rule of interpretation of the Constitution and the Statute is the same.

168. In this regard I want to cite the decision of Director of Taxation and Excise Govt, of E. Pak. (now Bangladesh) vs Mehedi Ali Khan Ponni 32 DLR (AD) 1980 138 wherein Chief Justice Kemal Uddin Hossain (as his Lordship then was) very succinctly made some observations which are relevant on the issue:

"Interpretation of Taxing Statute-Doctrine of LAISSEZ_ FAIRE AND WELFAIRE ECONOMY in interpreting a taxing Statute a controversy often arises and learned authorities are cited in support of the proposition that a taxing Statute is to be construed strictly in favour of the subject. But this view though not abandoned in case of unresolved ambiguity, does no longer get the one-sided support from the judicial authorities. The view of strict construction prevailed at a time when the doctrine of LAISSEZ FAIRE AND WELFAIRE ECONOMY was the ruling principle of a economy of a State, but almost all the leading States of the World have long abandoned the doctrine and adopted welfare doctrine of economy. Even a country like England where the doctrine of LAISSEZ FAIRE and WELFAIRE ECONOMY originated has abandoned it in favour of welfare economy. The newly emerging nations like ours have mostly adopted the welfare doctrine."

His Lordship then rightly observed:

"In a fiscal or taxing Statute one has to look merely at what is clearly said therein, for there is no room for any intendment nor for any equity or for any presumption. In case of unresolved ambiguity, it may be interpreted favourably to the citizen but nothing more. The attempt of the Court in case of ambiguity is to be guided by principle of justice and fairness and to try to arrive at a true meaning of the word."

169. I have found no ambiguity of any kind to hold that charging of minimum tax upon firm and company as provided in section 16CCC of the Ordinance should be viewed being unreasonable.

170. Much emphasis have been given upon Article 7 of the Constitution of Bangladesh from the Bar in that the enactment of section 16CCC of the Ordinance violated the primacy and supremacy of the Constitution that all powers in the Republic belonging to the people and they are exercised on behalf of the People shall be effected only under, and by the authority of this Constitution and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. My learned brother Justice Rahman accepted this argument viewing the same in juxtaposition with Article 26 of the Constitution that says laws inconsistence with the fundamental rights to be void.

171. To my interpretation Article 7 which is the awe inspiring mandate of the Constitution is specifically related to uphold the fundamental rights of the citizen. In no way it can form the basis of interpreting a fiscal Statute holding the same to be unconstitutional. The enactment in question has its bearing merely upon firm and company those who are doing business making profit and loss (as the case may be) certainly dealing with the public money, therefore, by any stretch of imagination it cannot be said that the imposition of minimum tax under section 16CCC is unjustified on the score that it has curtailing effect upon Article 7 of the constitution.

172. The discussions as made herein before and hereinafter would abundantly focus on the views that I expressed.

173. According to Maxwell, the function of a Court is to interpret a Statue according to the intent of the legislature and in doing so it must bear in mind that its function is jus dicere not jus dare: meaning thereby, the words of a Statue must not be overruled by the judges, but the reform of the law must be left in the hands of the Parliament. This view finds support in the case of Mohammad Ismail vs State 21 DLR (SC) 161 as it has already been quoted above.

174. In Commissioner of Sales Tax vs Parson Tools and Plant (1975) 45CC 22 it was held that the will of the legislature is the supreme law of the land and which demands absolute obedience. "Judicial power is never exercised", said Marshall CJ of the United States, "for the purpose of giving effect to the will of the Judges; always for the purpose of giving effect to the will of the legislature; or in other words to the will of the law." In the construction of the Statute Courts of Bangladesh are to ascertain the intention of the Parliament. The Courts of Bangladesh are to apply the law as expressed by the legislature.

175. In the case of SA Maroon vs Collector of Customs 11 DLR (SC) 200 it was observed:

"All Rules of interpretation have been devised as aids to the discovery of the legislative intents behind an enactment. Where the words are plain and unambiguous, that intent can best be judged by giving full effect to the ordinary grammatical meaning of those words. But when this is not the case an attempt should be made to discover the true intent by considering the relevant provision in the context of the whole Act in which it  appears and by having regard to the circumstances in which the enactment came to be  passed.  The previous state of the law, the mischief sought to be suppressed and the new remedy provided are relevant factor to be given due consideration."

176. The Indian Supreme Court also echoed in the like manner in Nasiruddin vs Shita Ram AIR 2003 (SC) 1543 and maintained:

"The Court's Jurisdiction to interpret a Statute can be invoked when the same is ambiguous. It is well known in a given case the court can iron out the fabric. It cannot change texture of the fabric. It cannot enlarge the scope of legislation or intention when the language of the provision is plain and unambiguous. It cannot add to or subtract words to a Statute or read something into it which is not there. It cannot re-write or recast legislation. It is also necessary to determine that there exists a presumption that the legislature has not used any superfluous words. It is well settled that the real intention of the legislation must be gathered from the language used. It may be true that use of the expression 'shall or may is not decisive for arriving at a finding as to whether Statute is directory or mandatory. But the intention of the legislature must be found out from the scheme of the Act. It is also equally well settled that when negative words are used the Court will presume the intention of the legislature was that the provisions are mandatory in character."

177. Section 16CCC begins with a non-obstante clause confirming a mandatory implication of the provision. A non-obstante clause is usually used in a provision to indicate that, that provision should prevail despite anything to the contrary in the provision mentioned in such non-obstante clause.

178. Now I would like to dilate and diversify my deliberations upon few provisions of Ordinance and the Constitution which will further elucidate and fortify my interpretation on the issue. Section 2(34) of the Ordinance defines `Income'. It enjoins—

"Income" includes—

(a)	any income, profits or gains, from whatever source derived, chargeable to tax under any provision of this Ordinance under any head specified in section 20;

(b)	any loss of such income, profits Or gains;

(c)	the profits and gains of any business of insurance carried on by a mutual insurance association computed in accordance with paragraph 8 of the Fourth Schedule;

(d)	Any sum deemed to be income, or any income accruing or arising or received, or deemed to accrue or arise or to be received in Bangladesh under any provision of this Ordinance;

Provided.............

179. Section 2(34) of the Ordinance does not employ any specific definition of income, only we find it as an inclusive law aiming some specific areas to be added and included in the category of income. In various pronouncements income has been defined in different ways. Their Lordships of the Privy Council in the case of Shaw Wallace and Co. AIR 1932 PC 138 said—

"Income is periodical monetary return coming with some sort of regularity from definite source likened pictorially to the fruit of a tree or the crop of a field"

180. This definition of income has been struck down to a great extent by the Privy Council in the subsequent judicial pronouncements. But under section 2(34) income includes any loss of income, profit or a gain of a business. According to sub-clause (b) loss of income, profit or gains arising from whatever source is chargeable to tax under section 20 of the Ordinance is also income. Loss is also included in the expression "income" or "profits and gains" under charging section. In the case of CIT vs Komar Chand vs Prem Chand Ltd. 40 1TR 106 (SC) it is observed that it may be said in one sense that "profits and gains" is "plus income" and loss is "minus income". Thus loss is also income for the purpose of computation of total income.

181. Section 2(62) of the Ordinance on the other hand, defines "Tax" saying that tax means the income tax payable under this Ordinance and includes any additional tax, excess profit tax, penalty, interest, fee or other charges levyable or payable under this Ordinance. The word tax includes both income tax and super tax. It seems in order to relieve the superior Court from exercise in interpreting and giving the meaning to the word 'Tax' the meaning of the word made simpler by giving a definition to understand what tax really means in the context of income tax law in a given case.

182. On the other hand the word 'tax' has also been defined in art. 152(1) of the Constitution as follows:—

`Taxation' includes the imposition of any tax, rate, duty or impost, whether general, local or special, and 'tax' shall be construed accordingly. Thus the word 'tax' has been used in a comprehensive sense to include all money raised by taxation and includes those known as 'rates' or other charges levied by local authorities under statutory powers. A tax cannot be levied or collected merely by an executive fiat or action without there being a law to support the same. In the Indian jurisdiction there is a conflict of judicial opinion as to whether levy or collection of tax by usage is ruled out.

183. But there is no scope of any such conflict of opinion in Bangladesh as article 83 contains the expression by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament. Under article 83 not only the levy but also the collection of tax must be sanctioned by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament. The expression 'levy' includes creation of liability and fixation of its quantum and the expression collect refers to physical realization of tax.

184. In the case of A. Hannan vs Collector of Customs 40 DLR 273 it was held by the High Court Division that fixation of rate of duty is a function which has to be performed by Parliament and this function cannot be delegated and this constitutional power cannot be shared with any body. This view of High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division while dismissing the Government Appeal by the special leave in Collector of Customs vs A. Hannan 42 DLR (AD) 167. The language by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament in art 83 shows that a tax can be levied by an Act of Parliament or by somebody else under the authority of an Act of Parliament. The imposition cannot exceed what the statute authorizes and the tax must fall within the four corners of the statute.

185. Article 60 provides that Parliament shall by law confer on the local government bodies power to impose tax for local purposes. There is no reason to hold that the word 'tax' in art.83 and art.60 has been used in different senses. It is thus abundantly clear that 'tax' can be levied and collected by the government and local government bodies. The Constitution has used the expression 'tax' in a wide sense as can be seen from the definition given Art. 152(1).

186. Article 80 of Chapter II of the Constitution deals with legislative and financial procedure. Article 80(1) states—"Every proposal in parliament for making a law shall be made in the form of a Bill. Article 81(1) further states-in this part 'Money Bill' means a Bill containing only provision dealing with all or any of the following matters—"(a) The imposition, regulation, alteration, remission or repeal of any tax." Article 81(3) enjoins— "Every money Bill shall, when it is presented to the President for his assent, bear a certificate under the hand of the Speaker that it is a Money Bill, and such certificate shall be inclusive for all purposes and shall not be questioned in any Court."

Lastly. Article 83 concluded by saying—" No tax shall be levied or collected except by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament Pronouncement."

187. Section 16CCC came into force as a Money Bill by the Finance Act 2011. Therefore, it cannot be said that the section was inserted in the Ordinance not in accordance with law. Consequently, legality of the Finance Act inserting section 16CCC in the Ordinance cannot be questioned. It has been done totally within the Constitutional domain and competence. It shall certainly be construed in its restricted Constitutional imposition. In other words an Act of Constitutional exercise is the result of introduction of section 16CCC in the Ordinance. It cannot be, in any manner be inferred that the provisions of section 16CCC is against the spirit of Article 7 read with Article 26 of the Constitution.

188. In the case of Sheikh Abdus Sabur vs Returning Officer 41 DLR (AD) 30 leave was granted to consider the question whether the bar of disqualification under section 7(2)(g) of the Union Parishad Ordinance for seeking election is hit by the equality provision under Article 27 of the Constitution. By a unanimous decision the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal holding

Article 27 of the Constitution does not operate as a bar in that regard. Article 27 of the Constitution enshrined that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law.

Justice Afzal while concurring with Shahab-uddin, J observed,

"A law cannot be struck down merely because it fails to spell out the particular objective of a provision in the legislation itself. In the instant case the impugned clause (g) was brought in by the Local Government Laws (Amendment) Act 1987 (Act XXIII of 1987) apparently for the purpose of providing an additional disqualification for a person seeking election to an Union Parishad. For the purpose of withstanding a challenge to its Constitutionality as being violative of Article 27 it has to stand the test of justification for being attached to Local Government body election only the Court will presume the Constitutionality of a Statue until shown otherwise."

189. Justice Bhagwati in the case of RIB Garg vs Union of India AIR 1981 SC 2138 reiterated that "the presumption of Constitutionality is indeed so strong that in order to sustain it, the Court may take into consideration matters of common knowledge matters of common report, the history of the times and may assume every state of facts which can be conceived existing at the time of legislation"

190. Bhagwati, J further observed that—"Laws relating to economic activities should be viewed with greater latitude than laws touching civil rights such as freedom of speech, religion etc. Every legislation particularly in economic matters is essentially empiric and it is based on  experimentation or what one may call trial and error method and therefore it cannot provide for all possible situations or anticipate all possible abuses. There, may be crudities inequities in  complicated experimental economic legislation  but on that account alone it cannot be struck down as invalid."

191. Further the Constitution does not permit the Court to direct or advise the executive in matters of policy or to sermonize qua any matter which under the Constitution lies within the sphere of Legislature or executive, provided these authorities do not transgress their Constitutional limits or statutory powers. Besides the fundamental principle of State Policy cannot be Judicially enforceable: Kudrat Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319.

<u>192. In my assessment section 16CCC of the Ordinance is not only provision which is to be ranked as a beneficial Statute, but it is also for the betterment of the nation at large. To my mind striking the said provision down shall amount to a travesty of law and a judicial extravaganza certainly indulge in excesses.</u>

193. Tax evaders are enemy to the tax system. It is the duty of the Government to take administrative and legislative measures to combat tax evasion. Tax evasion happens in many ways including the misreporting of income and expenses, manufacturing of books of accounts, concealment of assets and liabilities etc. Apart from tax evasion, tax payers device various tax avoidance schemes in collaboration with accountants, tax advisors and other related parties. Such tax evasion and avoidance erodes tax base and hampers revenue collection thereby bringing serious threat to the fiscal health of a country.

194. Supreme Court of India in the case of Pooran Mal etc. vs. Director of Inspection AIR 348 (1974) SCR (2) 704 observed:

"One cannot possibly ignore how such evasions eat into the vitals of the economic, life of the community. It is a well known fact of our economic life that huge sums of unaccounted money are in the circulation endangering its very fabrics. In a country which has adopted high rates of taxes a major portion of the unaccounted money should normally fill the government coffers. Instead of doing so it distorts the economy. Therefore, in the interest of the community it is only right that the fiscal authorities should have sufficient powers to prevent tax evasion."

<u>195. In the face of widespread tax evasion by company and big non-company taxpayers, and in order to overcome "zero taxation", reduce tax inequality among corporate taxpayers (if some companies pay tax and others do not, there becomes a uneven tax treatment among them) and to ensure revenue adequacy, governments in many countries introduced the concept of Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) where taxpayers need to pay a minimum amount of tax if the tax liability under regular method falls short of a minimum amount of tax. This Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) concept is introduced for various reasons:</u>

<u>Under section 16CCC, tax department compares between taxation under regular method and taxation under alternative method. If tax liability calculated in regular method is higher than the tax liability calculated in alternative method, tax under regular method will prevail. On the other hand, if tax liability calculated in regular method is lower than the tax liability calculated in alternative method, tax under alternative method will prevail. Therefore, taxpayer's tax liability is absolutely "single". In calculating tax liability under 16CCC, any tax paid in advance, at source or under section 74 is duly given credit. Moreover, when any income of a taxpayer falls under the ambit of final settlement of tax liability section 82C tax, that income does not come under the ambit of section 16CCC. Thus, there is absolutely no scope for double taxation under section 16CCC.</u>

<u>196. Under section 16CCC, tax liability of taxpayers is calculated under regular method and alternative method (i.e. 0.3% of gross receipt). If the tax liability, as calculated under regular method falls short of the tax calculated under alternative method (i.e. 0.3% of gross receipt), alternative tax will prevail.</u>

197. The writ petitioners appear to have completely misconceived and misconstrued section 20 of the Ordinance, and the very concept of alternative minimum tax. Section 16CCC is fully consistent with the objective of the Ordinance, fully congruent with all other provisions of the tax law, and fully in line with international best tax practice.

198. Imposition of minimum tax is a modern tax concept. As a member of global tax community, Bangladesh also adopted this modern tax concept of alternative minimum tax, in the name of 'Minimum Tax'.

199. In the line with global best practice, minimum tax concept was first introduced in Bangladesh by Finance Act, 1997 for non-company taxpayers. For company tax payers minimum tax concept was introduced by Finance Act, 2006 inserting section 16CC in the Ordinance which was subsequently omitted by the Finance Act, 2008 and thereafter by Finance Act, 2011 section 16CCC was introduced making the same applicable upon a firm having a gross receipt of more than Taka 50 Lakh or a company tax payer and is charged @ 0.30% on 'gross receipts.'

200. Minimum tax has long been but part of the fiscal law both in Bangladesh and in other countries including India, Pakistan, USA, Singapore, Korea, France, Austria, Malaysia, Latvia, Colombia, Nigeria, Madagascar. Panama, Honduras, Tunisia, Senegal Island, and Ivory Coast.

<u>201. By introducing section 16CCC no object of the Ordinance and the Constitution has been infringed. It is an excellent piece of enactment goes with the contemporary fiscal World and their practice. Certainly some unscrupulous fraction out of our larger tax payers have been stopped by introducing a minimum tax paying system under the said law in an assessment year. Legislature did the right thing at the right moment. Before parting I would once again pronounce the salutary remark of Lord Denning with resounding effect that-"Silence is not an option when things are ill done". Re vs Metropolitan Police Commissioner (1968) 2 All ER 319.</u>

202. In the result, all the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rules are hereby recalled and vacated. The respondents are directed to take steps in accordance with law forthwith.

Md Ashraful Kamal J: I have had the advantage of going through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my Lord Mr Justice AFM Abdur Rahman and my Lord Mr Justice Md Ashfaqul Islam. I concur with the judgment and order passed by my Lord Mr Justice Md Ashfaqul Islam.

Order of the Court.

By the majority decisions, let these Rules Nisi be discharged. However, there shall be no order as to costs. The stay granted earlier in different writ petitions are hereby recalled.

End.

full_judgment:
Zinat Ara J: Identical questions of law and more or less similar facts are involved in Writ Petitions No. 2848 of 2015 and 2849 of 2015 and the parties are same. Therefore, these writ petitions have been heard together and are being disposed of by this common judgment.

2. In writ petition No. 2848 of 2015, the petitioner has called in question the legality of the order under নথি নং-৪/এলটিউ,মুসক/লি”অ্যাং/৯৭/বিএটিবি/দাবিনামা/২০১৪/১৪৮৫ dated 22-3-2015 passed by respondent No. 3 (Annexure-A to the writ petition) demanding Taka 699,37,69,049.80 as supplementary duty and VAT from the petitioner for the period from financial year 2009-2010 to 31st January of financial year 2012-2013 on the ground of being violative of the provisions of sections 5(2), 35, 36 and 55(1) of the মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ (hereinafter referred to as the VAT Act) read with rules 3(3) and (7) of the মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ (hereinafter stated as the VAT Rules).

3. In writ petition No. 2849 of 2015, the petitioner has called in question the legality of the order under নথি নং-৪/এলটিউ,মুসক/লি”অ্যাং/৯৮/বিএটিবি/দাবিনামা/২০১৪/১৪৮৬ dated 22-3-2015 (Annexure-A to the writ petition) passed by respondent No. 3 demanding Taka 798,24,23,593.01 as supplementary duty and VAT from the petitioner for the period between financial year 2009-2010 to 3 1st January of financial year 2012-2013 and the order under নথি নং-৪/এলটিউ,মুসক/লি”অ্যাং/৯৯/বিএটিবি/দাবিনামা/২০১৪/১৪৮৭ dated 22-3-2015 (Anne- xure-A-1 to the writ petition) passed by respondent No. 3 demanding Taka 426,53,05,66144 as supplementary duty and VAT from the petitioner for the period between February of financial year 2012-2013 to October of financial year 2013-2014 on the ground of being violative of the provisions of sections 5(2), 35, 36 and 55(1) of the VAT Act read with rules 3(3) and (7) of the VAT Rules.

Admitted Facts

4. The petitioner, British American Tobacco Bangladesh Company Limited, is a public company limited by shares and incorporated in Bangladesh. It carries on business as a manufacturer and supplier of tobacco products including cigarettes. The petitioner is the Bangladeshi subsidiary of the British American Tobacco Group, a multinational conglomerate headquartered in London, United Kingdom. The brands' names of the petitioner's manufactured products include amongst others are BENSON & HEDGES, JOHN PLAYER GOLD. LEAF, PALL MALL, CAPSTAN, STAR, SCISSORS, PILOT and BRISTOL. The petitioner is enlisted with Dhaka and Chittagong Stock Exchanges. Its majority share-holder is the British American Tobacco Group holding approximately 72% of its issued shares. The petitioner is registered with the মূল্য সংযোজন কর কর্তৃপক্ষ (the VAT authorities) under section 15 of the VAT Act having VAT registration No. 5071005896. The petitioner is liable to pay মূল্য সংযোজন কর (VAT) and সম্পূরক শুল্ক (supplementary duty) on its products i.e. cigarettes under the VAT Act.

Petitioner's Case

5. The petitioner's cases in both the writ petitions are more or less similar and so, the sum and substance thereof are described below together to avoid unnecessary repetition:—

The petitioner is liable to pay VAT and supplementary duty on it's product i.e. cigarettes on the basis of retail price in terms of section 5(3) of the VAT Act and accordingly, it has been paying VAT on such retail price on all of its products on the basis of price declarations submitted by it and as approved by the VAT authorities from time to time. The Government by Gazette Notification being No. এস,আর,ও নং-১৪৯-আইন/২০০১/৩১৪-মূসক dated 7th June, 2001 (shortly stated as the Notification), in exercise of its power as conferred by section 14(1) of the VAT Act, exempted four classes of cigarettes from payment of supplementary duty (SD) in manufacturing stage in excess of the various extents as mentioned in the Notification. Classification of cigarettes of all manufacturers is done into four categories with reference to retail price brackets of the cigarettes. The Notification had no reference for consideration of the quality, goodwill/ reputation and/or brand value of the cigarettes. There is also no legal provision for classification of the cigarettes for exemption under section 14(1) of the VAT Act. The petitioner for its BRISTOL and PILOT Brands Cigarettes submitted price declarations on 19-8-2009, 9-11-2009, 12-8-2010, 23-6-2011, 27-6-2011, 21-6-2012 and 25-6-2012 to respondent No. 3, the Commissioner, Large Tax Payer's Unit (VAT) (hereinafter stated as the VAT Commissioner). The price declarations were approved under rule 3(3) of the VAT Rules within fifteen days on 10-9-2009 and 30-11-2009. Thereafter, by General Order dated 23-12-2013 (hereinafter stated as the General Order) of the National Board of Revenue (NBR), the price declarations were approved on 26-8-2010, 16-10-2010, 13-7-2011 and 2-7-2012. There was/is no scope under the VAT Act for testing the quality of the goods while approving the price declarations. According to price declarations and approval, the BRISTOL and PILOT Brand  Cigarettes fell in the lower price categories of the four classes as mentioned in the Notification. The VAT authorities received complaint from local cigarette manufacturers that BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes were, in fact, medium categories cigarettes, but declared as low price categories cigarettes causing huge loss to the national revenue. NBR considering its General Order dated 23-12-2010 issued Memo dated 28-11-2012 clarifying the matter. Respondent No. 4, the Additional Commissioner, Large Tax Payer's Unit (VAT) then submitted a report dated 12-2-2013 re-iterating the complaint. In the report, it was mentioned that the cause of huge deficit in the revenue earned from cigarettes was due to increase of the supply of BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes of lower price category by 259.28% upto October, 2013 compared with the period upto October, 2012. Thereafter, samples of STAR, BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes were collected from the petitioner's factory and sent to BCSIR for preparing a comparative statement of quality of BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes with STAR Brand Cigarettes, also manufactured by the petitioner as a medium price category cigarettes. No sample of cigarettes manufactured by local manufacturers was collected for comparative test or statement. BCSIR had sent a chemical examination report dated 10-1-2013 to the respondents stating that the PILOT, BRISTOL and STAR Brands Cigarettes were similar. According to the report of respondent No. 4 dated 12-2-2013, supplementary duty (SD) and VAT were calculated ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ রাজস্ব as on account of BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes for the period between January 2009-2010 to 2012- 2013, 2009-2013 and February 2012-2013 to October 2013-2014 by treating BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes in the medium price category. The respondents admitted that the petitioner submitted price declarations of BRISTOL Brand Cigarette and PILOT Brand Cigarette, VAT authorities approved the price declarations, the approval of the price declarations were supported by the General Order and the petitioner paid VAT and supplementary duty as approved by the price declarations. Therefore, the petitioner had/has no arrear VAT and SD to be paid, as there is no instance of (a) nonpayment of VAT by the petitioner, (b) refund of VAT received by the petitioner, (c) drawback of VAT by the petitioner and (d) adjustment being made by the petitioner or any act as provided in section 37(2) of the VAT Act or mistake or incorrect explanation. In the circumstances, the petitioner cannot be alleged to have committed an offence under section 37(2)(jha) of the VAT Act. In exercise of rule 3(7) of the VAT Rules, respondent No. 3 fixed the price of BRISTOL Brand Cigarettes as medium category. Upon issuance of such order, the petitioner ceased production, sale and supply of BRISTOL Brand Cigarettes and also filed an appeal against the order dated 31-1-2013, which is pending in the Appellate Tribunal, constituted under section 42 of the VAT Act. The petitioner recently came to know that by Memo under নথি নং-৫(১)মূসক নীতি ও বাজেট/২০০৮/৪৬৬ dated 2-10-2013, NBR, under the signature of respondent No. 7, upon reference to the sale of BRISTOL Brand and PILOT Brand Cigarettes by the petitioner, sought for an opinion from the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs (shortly, the Ministry of Law) as to whether it would be legal and justified to retrospectively subject a lower price category cigarette to VAT and SD on the basis of price applicable to medium price category cigarette. From the said Memo of respondent No. 7, it is evident that NBR sought for opinion from the Ministry of Law, but it made the demand without obtaining such legal opinion, though respondent No. 2 incorrectly stated that the demand was made on the basis of advice of the Ministry of Law. A demand notice was issued by respondent No. 3 upon the petitioner in Nothi No. 4/LTU-Mushak/A n/97/BATB/Dabnam a/13/9625 dated 24-11-2013 (shortly stated as demand letter dated 24-11-2013) for BRISTOL Brand Cigarettes under section 55(1) of the VAT Act demanding current register (Mushak-18) adjustment/payment of Taka 699,37,69,049.80 as ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ রাজস্ব (revenue loss) from the petitioner. Similarly, respondent No. 3 issued demand notice upon the petitioner in Nothi No. 4/LTU-Mushak/Ain/98/BATB/Dabinama/13/9626 dated 24-11-2013 (shortly stated as the demand letter dated 24-11-2013) and demand letter in Nothi No. 4/LTU-Mushak/Ain/99/ BATB/Dabinama/13/ 9627 dated 24-11-2013 (shortly stated as the demand letter dated 24-11-2013) demanding Taka 798,24,23,593.01 and Taka 426,53,05,661.44 respectively as SD, and VAT as revenue loss for PILOT Brand Cigarette for the period between 2009 to January, 2013 and February 2012-2013 to October 2013-2014 under section 55(1) of the VAT Act. The petitioner being aggrieved filed Writ Petitions No. 12496 of 2013 and 12497 of 2013 before the High Court Division and Rule Nisi were issued in the matters with orders of stay. The Government of Bangladesh then filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No. 233 of 2014 and CPLA No. 234 of 2014 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division. Eventually, by separate judgment and order dated 7-4-2014, the Appellate Division disposed of the leave petitions with a direction to hear and dispose of the writ petitions by the Division Bench presided over by Justice Zinat Ara and the ad-interim orders of stay passed by the High Court Division were stayed. Subsequently, the said writ petitions were disposed of by the High Court Division by judgment dated 21-5-2014 with a direction upon respondent No. 3 to decide the matters under section 55(3) of the VAT Act considering the objection raised by the petitioner. Meanwhile, the petitioner requested respondent No. 3 to withdraw the demand letters. Respondent No. 9 the Secretary, Ministry of Law, opined that the provision of the VAT Act and the rules framed thereunder do not permit retrospective imposition and recovery of VAT and SD, particularly, when the price declarations of the petitioner were duly approved by respondents No. 3 to 5 on year to year basis. Challenging the said opinion of respondent No. 9, one Dr. Md Moshiur Rahman filed Writ Petition No. 2077 of 2013 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division on 4-3-2015 issued a Rule Nisi and stayed the operation of the letter dated 12-2-2015. Against the said order, the petitioner filed Civil Miscellaneous Petition No. 214 of 2015 before the Appellate Division, which is pending. The petitioner also filed Writ Petition No. 2773 of 2015 before the High Court Division seeking a direction upon the respondents not to dispose of demand proceeding under section 55 of the VAT Act. The High Court Division issued Rule Nisi in the matter with an order of stay till 25-3-2015. Respondent No. 3 on 10-3-2015 heard the matter and issued letter on 12-3-2015 to the first Secretary NBR to appear and make submissions in favour of the VAT Authority. VAT is an indirect tax and there is no provision for collecting VAT beyond the approved price and the petitioner having paid VAT and other taxes on the basis of approved price, the demand asking the petitioner to pay VAT is unlawful. In view of the stay order passed in Writ Petition No. 2773 of 2015, respondent No. 3 had no authority to pass the impugned adjudication/assessment orders under section 55(3) of the VAT Act in the matters. Respondent No. 3 on total misconception of sections 55(1) and (3) of the VAT Act and rules 3(3) and (7) of the VAT Rules has arrived at erroneous findings that the petitioner has given false declarations violating the provision of sections 5, 26(ka), 35, 36 and 55 of the VAT Act read with rules 3(3) and (7) of the VAT Rules while passing the impugned orders. The impugned orders are violative of the fundamental right of the petitioner as guaranteed in article 31 of the Constitution.

Respondent No. 3's Case

6. Respondent No. 3 contested the Rules by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition denying and controverting the assertions made against this respondent and stating more or less similar facts. To avoid unnecessary repetition, those facts are summarized below:—

After approval of price declarations submitted by the petitioner, subsequently, it was found that the petitioner with mis-declaration presented untrue information in the declaration form Mushak-land managed to get it approved. Respondent No. 3, at his own motion, in exercise of power conferred by rule 3(7) of the VAT Rules, upon investigation and on the basis of test report acquired from BCSIR, found ample reason to re-fix the price of BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes to upper segment of value base. The petitioner although questioned the propriety of such re-fixation, but could not get any decision in his favour from any appellate authority. The petitioner could not adduce any reason as to why it stopped production of BRISTOL Brand Cigarettes and, as such, it is apparent that the impugned orders passed by respondent No. 3 are lawful. The demand has been evolved due to evasion of VAT by way of mis-declaration of actual price. The price declarations were approved provisionally with a condition set in Mashuk-1 formulated under rule 3 of the VAT Rules. The condition set forth in the foot note of Mashuk-1 is as under:—

“উল্লিখিত বিধিমালার বিধি-৩ বর্ণিত পরিস্থিতির আলোকে মূল্য সংযোজন কর কর্তৃপক্ষ কর্তৃক পরিচালিত কোন তদন্তে বা জরিপে উপরি-উক্ত ঘোষিত মূল্য ভিত্তি অসঙ্গগতিপূর্ণ বা কম প্রতিয়মান হওয়ার ক্ষেত্রে উক্ত কর্তৃপক্ষ কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত মূল্য ভিত্তি অনুযায়ী ঘোষণা প্রদানের তারিখ হইতে কর প্রদানে আমি বাধ্য থাকিব।”

7. Moreover, it is evident from price approval letter dated 30-6-2013 that the concerned Divisional Officer approved the price subject to some conditions, which is as under:—

“তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, যদি ভবিষ্যতে তদন্তে দাখিলকৃত মূল্য তথ্যে কোন অসংগতি বা অসত্য তথ্য পরিলক্ষিত হয় এবং এজন্য যদি কোন সরকারি রাজস্ব প্রাপ্য হয় তাহলে গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অনুকুলে উক্ত প্রার্থক্যজনিত রাজস্ব জমা প্রদান করতে বাধ্য থাকবেন।”

8. Therefore, the petitioner has supplied its product conceding the pre-condition as laid down in the approval order. It is mandatory for the petitioner to deposit the sum found to be not paid in course of investigation/enquiry due to untrue/misdeclaration in respect of BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes. From the letter dated 10-9-2009 bearing Nathi No. 4/LTU(Mushak)/ 25/British/Tobacco/Mu: Anu:/Bibhag/Part-1/06/- 3791, it transpires that the representative of the petitioner stated that the Brands BRISTOL and PILOT are not being marketed or sold in any other country of the world. Such a statement is nothing but a gross misrepresentation inasmuch as these brands belong to principal of the petitioner company and being marketed and sold by their principal's subsidiaries in rest of the world e.g. South America, Middle East, etc. Furthermore, these brands are being marketed and sold in India at a price of Rs. 47 which is same as CAPSTAN Brand cigarette, which is a high segment cigarette of the petitioner company. Moreover, the Brands BRISTOL and PILOT are being sold in the international market at much higher price as evidenced in the pricing available in the online duty free shops. In the price approvals issued by the respondents from time to time, it has been clearly mentioned that if in any investigation in future it is found that any information provided in the submitted pricing information is not true or inconsistent then the petitioner shall be bound to pay the taxes. Respondent No. 3, upon directions of their lordships in Writ Petitions No. 12496 of 2013 and 12497 of 2013, proceeded to determine the demand finally under section 55(3) of the VAT Act by applying judicial mind. The learned Advocate's certificate issued in respect of Writ Petition No. 2773 of 2015 was received by respondent No. 3 after this respondent had signed the note of the impugned orders on 19-3-2015 and 22-3-2015 at the early hours and dispatch thereof. Respondent No. 3 has not issued the impugned orders after seeing the lawyer's certificate. Moreover, respondent No. 3 was not also in a position to consider the application to adjourn the

proceedings of adjudication in view of the directions passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petitions No. 12496 of 2013 and 12497 of 2013. The instant writ petitions are not maintain-able inasmuch as the orders were passed by respondent No. 3 under section 55(3) of the VAT Act and such orders are appealable orders under section 42 of the VAT Act and, as such, there being equally efficacious alternative remedy, the Rules are liable to be discharged. The VAT authority is empowered to demand VAT which has not been paid for any reason within a period of five years. The VAT authority has rightly issued the demand notices under section 55(1) of the VAT Act and passed the impugned adjudication/ assessment orders under section 55(3) of the VAT Act. The writ petitions are misconceived and not maintainable and the Rules are, thus, liable to be discharged.

Arguments of the Contending Parties

9. Mr Sheikh Fazle Nur Taposh, the learned Advocate for the petitioner appearing with Mr AM Aminuddin, Mr Munshi Moniruzzaman, Mr Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury and Mr Selim Jahangir takes us through the writ petitions, the connected materials on record and the provisions of section 55(3) of the VAT Act and rules 3(3) and (7) of the VAT Rules and put forward the following arguments before us:—

(1) in Writ Petition No. 2773 of 2015 the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi and stayed the adjudication/ assessment proceeding pending before respondent No. 3 under section 55(3) of the VAT Act till 25-3-2015. The order of stay was communicated through lawyer's certificate to the respondents on 22-3-2015 at 9-30 am and so, respondent No. 3 had no authority to pass any order in the matter, but this respondent passed the impugned orders unlawfully;

(2) admittedly, prices were declared by the petitioner on 19-8-2009, 9-11-2009, 12-8-2010, 23-6-2011, 27-6-2011, 21-6-2012 and 25-6-2012 and those were approved by respondent No. 5 on 26-8-2009, 10-9-2009, 30-11-2009, 13-7-2011 and 2-7-2012 for BRISTOL and PILOT Brand Cigarettes. Therefore, the petitioner had supplied its products on payment of VAT on the approved prices, as there was no provision for modification of price approved after fifteen days. So, the demand of VAT by modifying the approval on 24-11-2013 i.e. after three years from the date of approval of price declarations is unlawful and barred by limitation;

(3) there is no provision to enhance the price declaration of products on 24-11-2013 and demand VAT on the enhanced price with retrospective effect from 19-8-2009;

(4) the demand of VAT by enhancing the price long after sale of the products does not come within the purview of section 55 of the VAT Act, as there was no allegation of evasion of VAT by the petitioner. Respondent No. 3 on total misconception of the provisions of sections 55(1) and (3) of the VAT Act and the rules 3(3) and (7) of the VAT Rules has arrived at a wrong finding that the petitioner has given false price declarations;

(5) the impugned orders dated 22-3-2015 are malafide and arbitrary inasmuch as in absence of any allegation that the petitioner sold BRISTOL and PILOT Brands Cigarettes at a price higher than the declared price or that the cigarettes are medium price category cigarettes, it cannot be said that the petitioner has committed any offence under section 37(2)(Jha)(Da) [ধারা (৩৭(২)(ঝ)(ড) of the VAT Act;

(6) since there is no scope to demand VAT with retrospective effect under sections 3, 5(3), 37 and 55 of the VAT Act or rules 3(3) and (7) of the VAT Rules, the impugned orders dated 22-3-2015 passed by respondent No. 3 under section 55(3) of the VAT Act assessing Taka 699,37,69,049.80, Taka 798,24, 23,593.01 and Taka 426,53,05,661.44 as unpaid VAT (পরিহকারকৃত/ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ রাজস্ব) and issuing final demands accordingly, are without jurisdiction and therefore, the instant writ petitions are maintainable, although there is provision for filing appeal against the impugned orders.

10. In support of his submissions, Mr Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh relied on the decisions of the following cases:—

(i)	Lt. Col. Nawabzada Muhammad Amir Khan vs the Controller of Estate Duty, reported in 13 DLR(SC) 106;

(ii)	Bangladesh Power Development Board vs Md Asaduzzaman Sikder, reported in 9 BLC (AD) 1;

(iii)	Bangladesh Bank vs Zafar Ahmed Chowdhury reported in 56 DLR (AD) 175;

(iv)	Nagina Silk Mill, Lyallpur vs Income Tax Officer, A-Ward, Lyallpur, reported in 15 DLR (SC) 181;

(v)	Abdul Mannan vs Khaleda Mowati, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195;

(vi)	Assessing Officer, Narayangonj Range vs Burmah Eastern Ltd., reported in 34 DLR (AD) 29;

(vii)	Government of Bangladesh, represented by Comptroller and Auditor General of Bangladesh vs Abdul Latif Chowkder, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 29;

(viii)	Motiur Rahman and others vs. Chowdhury Md Mahfuzul Islam, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 104 and

(ix)	Bangladesh Legal Aid Services Trust vs Bangladesh, reported in 7 BLC (AD) I.

11. In reply, Mr SM Moniruzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of respondent No. 3, takes us through the affidavits-in-opposition, the impugned orders, relevant provisions of sections 5(2) & (3), 37, 42 and 55(3) of the VAT Act and rule 3 of the VAT Rules and advanced the following arguments before us:—

(a) there is specific provision for preferring an appeal under section 42 of the VAT Act against the orders passed by respondent No. 3 under section 55(3) of the VAT Act. Therefore, there is an equally efficacious alternative remedy available to the petitioner under the VAT Act and, as such, the instant writ petitions under article 102 of the Constitution without availing the appellate forum are not maintainable;

(b) in the order dated 23rd April, 2015 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 929 of 2015, it has been specifically observed by their lordships of the Appellate Division that "there is a statutory provision for filing appeal against the assessment by the revenue authority." Thus, the Appellate Division also observed that there is a forum of appeal against the orders passed by respondent No. 3 and, as such, the instant writ petitions are not maintainable on this count also;

(c) respondent No. 3 signed the impugned orders on 19-3-2015 and 22-3-2015 at the early hours of the office and those were duly dispatched before the lawyer's certificate in question came to the respondents' knowledge, which was received by the respondent's office on

22-3-2015 at 9-30 am. Moreover, there was specific directions from the High Court Division in Writ Petitions No. 12496 and 12497 of 2013 upon respondent No. 3 i.e. the VAT Commissioner to decide the matter under section 55(3) of the VAT Act considering the objection raised by the petitioner in accordance with law within 120 days from the date of receiving the copy of the judgment. Therefore, the impugned orders having been passed by respondent No. 3 following the directions of the High Court Division is within the jurisdiction of respondent No. 3 and it cannot be said that the orders were passed beyond jurisdiction;

(d) under section 55(3) of the VAT Act, the VAT authority has jurisdiction to demand VAT and supplementary duty within a period of five years through notice;

(e) after approval of the petitioner's price declarations, it was found on enquiry/ investigation that the petitioner got the price declarations approved by giving untrue declarations and thus, paid less VAT and supplementary duty to the Government and, as such, the demands were made lawfully within a period of five years. In Mashuk-1 form formulated under rule 3 of the VAT Rules, there is specific note that if the declaration made is found to be inconsistent or less on the basis of enquiry/investigation, the person registered under VAT Act is liable to pay the unpaid VAT from the date of price declarations;

(f) in the price declaration approval orders, conditions were also imposed that if in future, on investigation, it is found that there is any inconsistency or incorrect information given in the price declarations and if any additional Government revenue is to be paid for such declarations, in such case, concerned VAT registered person is liable to pay such difference in favour of the Government;

(g) as it was found on enquiry/ investigation that the petitioner gave incorrect price declarations about the category of cigarettes as "low price category" instead of "medium price category", the demands under section 55(1) of the VAT Act as well as the impugned orders passed under section 55(3) of the VAT Act are lawful;

(h) the orders passed by respondent No. 3 are for a period which falls within five years and, as such, it cannot be said that the impugned orders passed by respondent No. 3 are violative of the provision of section 55(3) of the VAT Act or that the demands were made with retrospective effect violating any provision of the VAT Act or the VAT Rules or that the impugned orders have been passed malafide:

(i) in the above facts and circumstances, the petitioner's remedy lies before the Appellate Tribunal under section 42 of the VAT Act and the petitioner has also an opportunity to file VAT appeal before the High Court Division, if aggrieved by the order of Appellate Tribunal under the said Act;

(j) in the above facts and circumstances of the cases as well as the provisions of law, it is evident that the impugned orders have been lawfully passed by respondent No. 3, VAT Commissioner and, as such, the Rules are liable to be discharged with costs.

12. In support of his submissions on non-maintainability of the instant writ petitions, Mr Moniruzzaman has relied on the decisions in the following cases:—

(i) Sharping Matshyajibi Samity vs Bangladesh, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 85;

(ii) Kartik Das Gupta vs Election Commission of Bangladesh, reported in 8 ADC 578 and

(iii) in the case of Oroscom Telecom Bangladesh Limited vs National Board of Revenue, Dhaka, reported in 63 DLR 442.

Point for Determination

13. In view of the arguments as advanced by the contending parties, the sole question to be decided in these Rules is the legality of the impugned orders.

Examination of the Records, etc.

14. We have examined the writ petitions, the affidavits-in-opposition, the impugned orders and the connected materials on record. We have also carefully studied the decisions as referred to by Mr Sheikh Fazle Nur Taposh, the learned Advocate for the petitioner and Mr SM Moniruzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney General.

Deliberation of the Court

15. In order to decide the legality of the impugned orders, it is necessary to examine the relevant portions of the impugned orders.

16. For the sake of better understanding, the said portions of the impugned order (Annexure-A to Writ Petition No. 2848 of 2015) is quoted below:—

“.................

১৪। দাবিনামাটি জারি করা হয়েছে BCSIR এর ১০-১-২০১৩ খ্রিঃ তারিখের পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনের ফলাফলের ভিত্তিতে। উক্ত পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনে ২১টি Test specification এর মধ্যে ১৭টির ক্ষেত্রে Star Filter King KSF এবং Bristol KSF এর same এবং ৪টির ক্ষেত্রে not same উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে এবং "Star Filter King KSF brand is more similar to Bristol style KSF brand” মর্মে মন্তব্য করা হয়েছে। উক্ত পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনের ভিত্তিতে স্টার ফিল্টার সিগারেটের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট সময়ের ঘোষিত মৃসক-১ এর পণ্য মূল্যের ভিত্তিতে বৃষ্টল হয়েছে। BCSIR এর পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনে উভয় ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটের ক্ষেত্রে টোব্যাকো গ্রেড স্থানীয়) ৪ চোর) উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে। ২০১২-১৩ অর্থবছরে স্টার সিগারেটের জন্য প্রতি কেজি তামাকের মূল্য (২১-৬-২০১২ খ্রিঃ তারিখে) ১৭৯.৭৭ টাকা এবং বৃষ্টল সিগারেটের জন্য প্রতি কেজি তামাকের মূল্য ১৬৮.৮৯ টাকা (২৫-৬-২০১২ খ্রিঃ তারিখে) মুসক-১ এ ঘোষণা করা হয়েছে। বৃহৎ করাদাতা ইউনিটের নথি থেকে দেখা যায়, বিভিন্ন সময়ে বৃষ্টল ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটের জন্য প্রতি কেজি টোব্যাকো মূল্য স্টার ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটের প্রতি কেজি টোব্যাকো মুল্যের চেয়ে কম ঘোষণা প্রদান করা হয়েছে। BCSIR এর পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনে স্টার ব্রান্ডে টোব্যাকো ফ্লেভারের ব্যবহার দেখা গেছে কিন্তু বিএটিবি কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত বার্ণিত মূল্য ঘোষণায় টোব্যাকো ফ্রেতারের ব্যবহার দেখানো হয় নাই। (এটিও মিথ্যা ঘোষণার একটি প্রমাণ) উক্ত মূল্য ঘোষণায় দেখা যায় উভয় ব্রান্ডের জন্য ব্রাংকাস এর ব্যবহারের পরিমাণ এবং বর্ণনা একই কিন্তু স্টার ব্রান্ডের ক্ষেত্রে প্রতি হাজার শলাকা সিগারেটের জন্য মূল্য ৫০.৯২ টাকা এবং বৃ্স্টলের ক্ষেত্রে প্রতি হাজার শলাকা সিগারেটের জন্য ৪৭.৬০ টাকা ঘোষণা দেয়া হয়েছে। একইভাবে BOPP PHS20 118mm HL Pack Wrap এর ক্ষেত্রে একই পরিমাণ উপকরণ ব্যবহার ঘোষণা করে, মুল্য স্টারের তুলনায় বৃষ্টলের ক্ষেত্রে কম ঘোষণা করা হয়েছে। বর্ণিত তথ্য প্রমাণ করে মিথ্যা ঘোষণার মাধ্যমে বৃষ্টলের উপকরণ মূল্য স্টারের উপকরণ মূল্যের সমান হওয়ার বাস্তব কারণ থাকা সত্বেও কম মূল্য ঘোষণা করে নি্ন মূল্যস্তরে রাখা হয়েছে। এছাড়া বৃস্টল ব্রান্ডের ক্ষেত্রে ওভারহেড খরচও স্টার ব্রান্ডের তুলনায় অনেক কম ঘোষণা করা হয়েছে। যার গ্রহণযোগ্য কোন যৌক্তিক কারণ খুঁজে পাওয়া যায় না। একই কারখানায় একই ধরনের লোকবল দিয়েই বিভিন্ন ব্রান্ডের সিগারেট উৎপাদন করা হয়। সিগারেট উৎপাদনের ক্ষেত্রে ব্রান্ডভিত্তিক লোকবল নিয়োগ করা হয় না। ব্রান্ডভিত্তিক ওভারহেড খরচের ব্যাপক পার্থক্যের সমর্থনে বিএটিবি গ্রহণযোগ্য কোন তথ্য উপস্থাপন করতে পারেনি । বৃষ্টল ব্রান্ডের মূল্য ঘোষণার ক্ষেত্রে বিএটিবি মিথ্যা ঘোষণা প্রদান করে নাই মর্মে গ্রহণযোগ্য কোন তথ্য/উপাত্ত কারণ দর্শানো নোটিশের জবাবে বা শুনানিকালে পেশ করে নাই ।

১৫। বর্ণিত পর্যবেক্ষণে থেকে বৃষ্টল ব্রান্��ের সিগারেটের মূল্য ঘোষণার ক্ষেত্রে বিএটিবি কর্তৃক মিথ্যা ঘোষণা প্রদানের বিষয়টি প্রমাণিত হয়। অর্থাৎ বিএটিবি মধ্যম মূল্যস্তরের সিগারেট হওয়া সত্বেও বৃষ্টল ব্রান্ড সিগারেটের নিম্ন  মূল্যস্তরের সিগারেট হিসাবে মিথা মূল্য ঘোষণা প্রদানের মাধ্যমে প্রদেয় সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসক পরিশোধ করে নাই ।

১৬। উপরে বর্ণিত পর্যবেক্ষণ অনুযায়ী বিএটিবি কর্তৃক মধ্যম মুল্যস্তরের বৃষ্টল ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটকে নিম্ন মূল্যস্তরের

সিগারেট হিসাবে যিথ্যা ঘোষণা প্রদানের মাধ্যমে সম্পুরক শুল্ক ও মূসক কম পরিশোধের বিষয়টি প্রতিষ্ঠিত হয়েছে। দাবিকৃত সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মুসক এর পরিমাণ/অংক নিয়ে প্রতিষ্ঠানটি কোন আপত্তি উ্থাপন করে নাই দাবিনামাটি মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৩৭ এর উপ-ধারা (২) এর দফা (ঝ) এবং (ড) এ বর্ণিত অপরাধ সংটনের কারনে জারি করা হয়েছে। দফা (ঝ) এ বর্মিত অপরাধ সংঘটনের মাধ্যমে কম পরিশোধিত সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মুসক আদায়ের ক্ষেত্রে সময়সীমা প্রযোজ্য নয়। (ধারা ৫৫ এর উপ-ধারা (১) এর শর্তাংশ), অর্থাৎ দাবিনামাটি জারি আইনসম্মত আছে।

১৭. বর্ণিত অবস্থায় বৃহৎ করদাতা ইউনিট, মূল্য সংযোজন কর এর নথি-8/LTU-মুসক/আইন/৯৭/বিএটিবি/দাবিনামা/ ১৩/৯৬২৫, তারিখ ২৪-১১-২০১৩ খিঃ এর মাধ্যমে মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫ এর উপ-ধারা (১) অনুযায়ী সম্পূরক শুদ্ধ বাবদ পাওনা ৫৮২,২৩,২৪,১৫৭.৭২ টাকা ও মূসক বাবদ ১১৭,১৪১৪৪৮৯২.১০ টাকাসহ মোট ৬৯৯,৩৭,৬৯,০৪৯.৮০ (ছয়শত নিরানব্বই কোটি সাইত্রিশ লক্ষউনসত্তর হাজার উনপঞাশ টাকা আশি পয়সা) টাকার দাবির পরিমাণ একই রেখে মুল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫ এর উপ-ধারা (৩) অনুযায়ী দাবিনামাটি চূড়ান্ত করা.হলো এবং এতদ্বারা চূড়ান্ত দাবিনামা জারি করা হলো।

১৮। দাবিকৃত সম্পূরক শুল্ক বাবদ পাওনা ৫৮২,২৩,২৪,১৫৭.৭২ টাকা ও মূসক বাবদ ১১৭,১৪,৪৪৮ ৯২.১০

টাকাসহ মোট ৬৯৯,৩৭,৬৯,০৪৯.৮০ (ছয়শত নিরানব্বই কোটি সাইত্রিশ লক্ষ উনসত্তর হাজার উনপঞ্চাশ টাকা আশি পয়সা) টাকা অবিলম্বে চলতি হিসাবে (মুসক-১৮) সমবয়ের মাধ্যমে সরকারি কোষাগারে জমা প্রদান করে তার প্রমাণসহ এ দপ্তরকে বাংলাদেশ কোম্পানী লিমিটেডকে অনুরোধ করা হলো ।”

17. Similarly, in Writ Petition No. 2849 of 2015, the following adjudication order (Annexure-A to the writ petition) was passed:-

১৪ । দাবিনামাটি জারি করা হয়েছে ১০-১-২০১৩ খ্রিঃ তারিখের পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনের ফলাফলের ভিত্তিতে। উক্ত পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনে  ২১টি Test specification এর মধ্যে ১৭টির ক্ষেত্রে Pilot Filter King KSF এবং Bristol KSF এর same এবং ৪টির ক্ষেত্রে not same উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে এবং “Pilot Filter King KSF grand is more similar to Bristol style KSF brand” মর্মে মন্তব্য করা হয়েছে। BCSIR Star Filter King KSF এর সাথে Bristol style KSF এর তুলনামুলক পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনের দিয়েছে । এই প্রতিবেদনেও ২১টি Test specification এর মধ্যে ১৭টির ক্ষেত্রে Star Filter King KSF এবং Bristol KSF এর same এবং ৪টির ক্ষেত্রে not same উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে এবং “Star Filter King KSF brand is more similar to Bristol style KSF brand” মর্মে মন্তব্য করা হয়েছে। তিনটি ব্রান্ডের যে ২১টি specification পরীক্ষা করা হয়েছে তা একই বর্ণনায় এবং তিনটি ব্রান্ডের মধ্যেই ১৬টি এর specification ফলাফল same এবং ৩টির ক্ষেত্রে not

same। ১টি specification এর ক্ষেত্রে (Aluminum Foil) শুধু স্টার এর সাথে তুলনায় পাইলটের ক্ষেত্রে বৃষ্টলের অনুরূপ নয়। অন্য সব ক্ষেত্রে স্টার ব্রান্ডের সাথে তুলনায় বৃষ্টল ও পাইলট ব্রান্ডের পরীক্ষার ফলাফল একই। উক্ত পরীক্ষার প্রতিবেদনের ভিত্তিতে স্টার ফিল্টার সিগারেটের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট সময়ের ঘোষিত মূসক-১ এর পণ্য মূল্যের ভিত্তিতে পাইলট ব্রান্ডের জন্য মূল্য বিবেচনায় নিয়ে পরিহারকৃত মূসক নির্ণয় করা হয়েছে। BCSIR এর পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনে পাইলট ও স্টার উভয় ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটের ক্ষেত্রে টোব্যাকো গ্রেড স্থানীয়) ৪ (চার) উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে । ২০১২-১৩ অর্থ বছরে স্টার সিগারেটের জন্য প্রতি কেজি তামাকের মূল্য (২১-৬-২০১২ খ্রিঃ তারিখে) ১৭৯.৭৭ টাকা এবং পাইলট সিগারেটের জন্য প্রতি কেজি তামাকের মূল্য ১৫৫.৮০ টাকা (২১-৬-২০১২) খ্রিঃ তারিখে) বৃহৎ করাদাতা ইউনিটের নথি থেকে দেখা যায়, বিভিন্ন সময়ে পাইলট ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটের জন্য তামাকের মূল্যের চেয়ে কম ঘোষণা  করা হয়েছে। BCSIR এর পরীক্ষা প্রতিবেদনে স্টার ব্রান্ডে টোব্যাকো ফ্লেভার ব্যবহার দেখা গেছে। কিন্তু উক্ত মূল্য ঘোষণায় স্টার ব্রান্ডে টোব্যাকো ফ্লেভার ব্যবহার দেখানো হয় নাই। (এটিও মিথ্যা ঘোষণার একটি প্রমাণ)। উক্ত মূল্য ঘোষণায় দেখা যায় যে, স্টার ও পাইলট ব্রান্ড উভয়ের ক্ষেত্রে সিগারেট পেপার ব্যবহারের পরিমাণ (ওজনে) একই, কিন্তু স্টার ব্রান্ডের ক্ষেত্রে প্রতি হাজার শলাকা সিগারেট পেপারের মূল্য ১৭.৭২ টাকা এবং পাইলটের ক্ষেত্রে প্রতি হাজার শলাকার জন্য ১৪.৭১ টাকা ঘোষণা দেয়া হয়েছে। একইভাবে BOPP PHS20 118 mm HL Pack Wrap, SRF 20SH2 Blanks এর ক্ষেত্রে একই পরিমাণ উপকরণ ব্যবহার ঘোষণা করে মূল্য স্টারের তুলনায় পাইলটের ক্ষেত্রে কম ঘোষণা করা হয়েছে। বর্ণিত তথ্য প্রমাণ করে মিথ্যা ঘোষণার মাধ্যমে পাইলটের উপকরণ মুল্য স্টারের উপকরণ মুল্যের সমান হওয়ার বাস্তব কারণ থাকা সত্ত্বেও কম মূল্য ঘোষণা করে নিম্ন মূল্যস্তরে রাখা হয়েছে। এছাড়াও পাইলট ব্রান্ডের ক্ষেত্রে ওভারহেড খরচও স্টার ব্রান্ডের তুলনায় অনেক কম ঘোষণা করা হয়েছে। যার গ্রহণযোগ্য কোন যৌক্তিক কারণ খুঁজে পাওয়া যায় না। একই কারখানায় একই ধরনের লোকবল দিয়েই বিভিন্ন ব্রান্ডের সিগারেট উৎপাদন করা হয়। সিগারেট উৎপাদনের ক্ষেত্রে ব্রান্ডভিত্তিক লোকবল নিয়োগ করা হয় না। ব্রান্ডভিত্তিক ওভারহেড খরচের ব্যাপক পার্থক্যের সমর্থনে বিএটিবি গ্রহণযোগ্য কোন তথ্য উপস্থাপন করতে পারেনি। পাইলট ব্রান্ডের মূল্য ঘোষণার ক্ষেত্রে বিএটিবি মিথ্যা ঘোষণা প্রদান করে নাই মর্মে গ্রহণযোগ্য কোন তথ্য/উপাত্ত কারণ দর্শানো নোটিশের জবাবে বা শুনানিকালে পেশ করে নাই।

১৫। বর্ণিত পর্যবেক্ষণ থেকে পাইলট ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটের মূল্য ঘোষণার ক্ষেত্রে বিএটিবি কর্তৃক মিথ্যা ঘোষণা প্রদানের বিষয়টি প্রমাণিত হয় । অর্থাৎ বিএটিবি মাধ্যম মুল্যস্তরের সিগারেট হওয়া সত্তেও পাইলট ব্রান্ড সিগারেটকে নিম্ন মূল্যন্তরের সিগারেট হিসাবে মিথ্যা মূল্য ঘোষণা প্রদানের মাধ্যমে প্রদেয় সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসক পরিশোধ করে নাই।

১৬। উপরে বর্ণিত পর্যবেক্ষণ অনুযায়ী বিএটিবি কর্তৃক মধ্যম মূল্যস্তরের পাইলট ব্রান্ডের সিগারেটকে নিম্ন মূল্যন্তরের সিগারেট হিসাবে খিথ্যা ঘোষণা প্রদানের মাধ্যমে সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসক কম পরিশোধের বিষয়টি প্রতিষ্ঠিত হয়েছে। দাবিকৃত সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মুসক এর পরিমাণ/অংক নিয়ে প্রতিষ্ঠানটি কোন আপত্তি উত্থাপন করে নাই। দাবিনামাটি মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৩৭ এর উপ-ধারা (২) এর দফা (ঝ) এবং (ড) এ বর্ণিত অপরাধ সংঘটনের কারণে জারি করা হয়েছে দফা (ঝ) এ বর্ণিত অপরাধ সংঘটনের মাধ্যমে কম পরিশোধিত সম্পূরক শুল্ক ও মূসক আদায়ের ক্ষেত্রে সময়সীমা প্রযোজ্য নয়। (ধারা ৫৫ এর উপ-ধারা (১) এর শর্তাংশ), অর্থাৎ দাবিনামাটি জারি আইনসম্মত আছে।

১৭। বর্ণিত অবস্থায় বৃহৎ করদাতা ইউনিট, মূল্য সংযোজন কর এর নথি-৪/LTU-মূসক/আইন/৯৮/বিএটিবি/দাবিনামা/১৩/৯৬২৬৫, তারিখ-২৪-১১-২০১৩ খিঃ এর মাধ্যমে মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫ এর উপ-ধারা (১)অনুযায়ী সম্পূরক শুল্ক বাবদ পাওনা  ৬৫৯,২১,৪৮,০১২.৩৬ টাকা ও মুসক বাবদ ১৩৯,০২,৭৫,৫৮০.৬৫ টাকাসহ মোট ৭৮৯,২৪,২৩,৫৯৩.০১ (সাতশত আটানব্বই কোটি চব্বিশ লক্ষ তেইশ হাজার পাঁচশত তিরানব্বই টাকা এক পয়সা) টাকার দাবির পরিমাণ একই রেখে মূল্য সংযোজণ কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫ এর উপ-ধারা (৩) অনুযায়ী দাবিনামাটি চূড়ান্ত করা হলো এবং এতদ্বারা চুড়ান্ত দাবিনামা জারি করা হলো।

১৮। দাবিকৃত সম্পূরক শুদ্ক বাবদ প��ওনা পাওনা ৬৫৯,২১১৪৮,০১২,৩৬ টাকা ও মূসক বাবদ ১৩৯,০২,৭৫,৫৮০.৬৫ টাকাসহ মোট ৭৮৯,২৪,২৩,৫৯৩,০১ (সাতশত আটানব্বই কোটি চব্বিশ লক্ষ তেইশ হাজার পাঁচশত তিরানব্বই টাকা এক পয়সা) টাকা অবিলম্বে চলতি হিসাবে (মূসক-১৮) সমবয়ের মাধ্যমে সরকারি কোষাগারে জমা প্রদান করে তার প্রমাণসহ এ দপ্তরকে লিখিতভাবে অবহিত করার করা জন্য বৃটিশ আমেরিকান টোব্যাকো বাংলাদেশ কোম্পানি লিমিটেডকে অনুরোধ করা হলো।”

18. In Writ Petition No. 2848 of 2015, before passing the aforesaid adjudication order, a demand letter dated 24-11-2013 was served upon the petitioner.

19. Relevant portion of which is as under:-

“০৮ উপরে-বর্ণিত হিসাব অনুযায়ী মধ্যম মূল্য স্তরের সিগারেটকে নিম্ন মূল্য স্তরে অসত্য ঘোষণা প্রদানের বিষয়টি মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৩৭২) এর (ঝ) ও (ড) এর সুস্পষ্ট লংঘন । উল্লিখিত বিধান লংঘনপূর্বক সরকারের প্রাপ্য রাজস্ব পরিহার করায় তা আদায়যোগ্য এবং আইনানুগ ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণীয়। সুতরাং, মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর ধারা ৫৫১) অনুযায়ী গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকারের পক্ষে ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ রাজস্ব বাবদ ৬৯৯,৩৭,৬৯,০৪৯,৮২ (ছ্য়শত নিরানববই কোটি সাইত্রিশ লক্ষ উনসত্তর হাজার উনপঞ্চাশ টাকা বিরাশি পয়সা) টাকা আপনার প্রতিষ্ঠানের নিকট থেকে আদায়ের জন্য প্রাথমিক দাবিনামা জারি করা হলো। দাবিকৃত অর্থ এ নোটিশ জারির দশ (১০) কার্যদিবসের মধ্যে চলতি হিসাব (মুসক-১৮) এ সময় বা সরকারি কোষাগারে জমা করে তার প্রমাণক (টি আর-৬) এ দপ্তরে দাখিলের জন্য অনুরোধ করা হলো ।”

20. Prior to issuance of this final demand after adjudication, similar show cause notice was issued upon the petitioner relating to the other writ petition.

21. Now, let us examine the relevant provisions of the VAT Act i.e. section 55 of the VAT Act and rule 3 of the VAT Rules.

22. For better understanding, the said provisions of law are quoted below:-

section 55 of the VAT Act in the financial year 2009-2010.

“ধারা ৫৫।- অনাদায়ী ও কম পরিশোধিত যুল্য সংযোজন কর সহ অন্যান্য শুল্ক-কর আদায় ।- (১) যে ক্ষেত্রে কোনো ব্যক্তির পণ্য সরবরাহ বা প্রদত্ত সেবার উপর প্রদেয় মূল্য সংযোজন কর বা, ক্ষেত্রমত, মূল্য সংযোজন কর ও সম্পূরক শুন্ধ কোনো কারণবশত ধার্য বা পরিশোধ করা হয় নাই বা কম ধার্য বা কম পরিশোধ করা হইয়াছে অথবা  ভুলবশত ফেরত প্রদান করা হইয়াছে বা ধারা ১৩ এর অধীন মূল্য সংযোজন কর, সম্পূরক শুল্ক, আমদানি শুন্ক, আবগারি শুল্ক, অন্যান্য শুল্ক ও কর (আগাম আয়কর ব্যতীত), ভুলবশত প্রত্যর্পণ করা হইয়াছে বা বাংলাদেশে সরবরাহকৃত কোনো পণ্য বা সেবার উপর প্রদেয় কর বা শুল্কের বিপরীতে ভুলবশতঃ বা ভুল ব্যাখ্যার কারণে সমবায় করা হইয়াছে, সেই ক্ষেত্রে উক্ত ব্যক্তিকে তাহার উপর যে তারিখে উক্ত শুল্ক ও মূল্য সংযোজন কর প্রদেয় হইয়াছিল বা কম পরিশোধিত হইয়াছিল বা ফেরত প্রদান করা হইয়াছিল বা প্রত্যর্পণ করা হইয়াছিল বা সমবয় করা হইয়াছিল সেই তারিখ হইতে তিন বৎসরের মধ্যে সংশ্লিষ্ট মূল্য সংযোজন কর কর্মকর্তা নোটিশ ছারা নোটিশে উল্লেখিত শুন্ধ বা মূল্য সংযোজন কর দাবী করিয়া উহাতে উল্লিখিত সময় সীমার মধ্যে উক্ত শুন্ক বা মূল্য সংযোজন কর পরিশোধের জন্য কারণ দর্শানো নোটিশ জারি করিবেন”

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, সেক্ষেত্রে কোন নিবন্ধিত ব্যক্তি বা প্রতিষ্ঠান কর ফীকি দেওয়ার উদ্দেশ্যে কোন তথ্য গোপন করেন,

বিকৃতি করেন বা মিথ্যা তথ্য প্রদান পূর্বক মূসক রেজিস্ট্রার, চলতি হিসাব বা কর চালানপত্র ইস্যু করেন, সেইক্ষেত্রে, আত্মপক্ষ সমর্থনের সুযোগ এবং যুক্তি সংগত শুনানি প্রদানের পর উদ্দেশ্যমূলক অপরাধ প্রমাণিত হইলে এই উপ-ধারা অধীন ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণের ক্ষেত্রে উহাতে উল্লিখিত তিন বৎসর সময়সীমা উক্ত ব্যক্তির উপর প্রযোজ্য হইবে না বা সংশ্লিষ্ট মূল্য সংযোজন কর কর্মকর্তা উক্ত ব্যক্তির উপর দাবী করার ক্ষেত্রে বারিত হইবেন না।

(২) আমদানীকৃত পণ্যের ক্ষেত্রে কোনো মূলা সংযোজন কর বা, ক্ষেত্রমত, মূল্য সংযোজন কর ও সম্পূরক শুল্ক, কোনো কারণবশতঃ পরিশোধ করা না হইয়া থাকিলে বা ভুলবশত কম পরিশোধিত হইয়া থাকিলে বা ফেরত প্রদত্ত হইয়া থাকিলে উহা Customs Act 44 section 32 cs ame fad wait আদায় করা হইবে।

(৩) উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন শুল্ক ও কর প্রদানের জন্য যেই ব্যক্তির নিকট হইতে দাবী করা হয় সেই ব্যক্তি লিখিতভাবে উক্ত দাবীর বিরুদ্ধে আপত্তি উত্থাপন করিলে তাহাকে শুনানির সুযোগ দান করিতে হইবে । অতঃপর উক্ত ব্যক্তির উত্থাপিত আপত্তি বিবেচনা করিয়া সংশ্লিষ্ট মূল্য সংযোজন কর কর্মকর্তা নোটিশে দাবীকৃত শুল্ক ও করের পরিমাণ প্রয়োজনবোধে পুনঃ

নির্ধারণ করিতে পারিবেন, এবং উক্ত ব্যক্তির নোটিশে দাবীকৃত বা ক্ষেত্রমত পুনঃনির্ধারন শুন্ক ও কর পরিশোধ করিতে বাধ্য থাকিবেন।

(৪) উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন শুল্ক ও কর প্রদানের জন্য যেই ব্যক্তির নিকট হইতে দাবী করা হয়, সেই ব্যাক্তি লিখিতভাবে উক্ত দাবীকৃত অর্থ কিস্তিতে পরিশোধের ইচ্ছ ব্যক্ত করিলে কমিশনার তৎ্কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত শর্ত পরিশোধের জন্য আদেশ প্রদান করিতে পারিবেন” তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কিস্তি প্রদানের সময়সীমা ছয় মাসের অতিরিক্ত হইবে না।” Rule 3 of the VAT Rules.
