It is further submitted that the layout plan shows an open space in front of Road No. 20, thus making a representation to the lessees on that road that the open space will remain. The learned Advocate has referred to the decision in the case of Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakhya and another vs Mohshinul Islam and another reported in 53 DLR (AD) 79 and submitted that RAJUK can develop new sites, but not at the expense of open spaces. She also referred to the unreported decision of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1046 of 1993, (which was upheld by the Appellate Division) which held that the respondents could make alteration for improvement schemes, but keeping the open spaces intact.

 8. The learned Advocate for BELA further submitted that the layout plan is part of the master plan and cannot be deviated from without following the procedures laid down in sections 69, 73 and 74 of the Town Improvement Act.

 9. In support of the petitioner's case, the case of Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakhya and another vs Mohshinul Islam and another reported in 11 BLT (AD) 56, was referred wherein it was held that, although under section 40(b) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 RAJUK may alter the layout plan, this power must be exercised for the purposes of improvement. It was submitted that in the instant case there was no improvement and, on the contrary, open space, greenery and pollution free atmosphere was being taken away. 

10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the RAJUK, and also representing the added respondent in WP 948 of 1997, submitted that the layout plan for the 6 additional plots is a continuation of the earlier plan to incorporate underdeveloped land. The learned Advocate referred to the decision in Writ Petition No. 1001 of 1993 and submitted that in that writ petition the High Court did not interfere with the allotments, which had taken place prior to the filing of the writ petition. He further submitted that the land, where the additional plots were reclaimed was not earmarked as open space or park, nor any area of the lake was reduced as a result of the reclamation. He further referred to the decision in the case of Chairman, RAJUK and others vs Parvin Akhter reported in 7 BLC (AD) 167 where it was held that the petitioners did not get any vested right to have open space between her house and the lake. He further submitted that there is no evidence that the lake has in any way been reduced in size as a result of the additional plots and the new Road No. 22. The learned Advocate submits that the petitioner knew about the revised plan in November, 1995 but did not challenge the same at that time. Referring to the application by the added respondent in WP No. 5121 of 1996, he submitted that the new plots were allotted on 25-10-1995, whereas the writ petition was filed on 24-11-96. He further submitted that the petitioners have not produced any Master Plan to show how there has been any unauthorised deviation from it. In fact, as was found in the 7 BLC case, there is no separate Master Plan for the new development schemes. He went on to submit that the revised layout plan has been authorised as has been sworn by the respondent in his affidavit-in-opposition, which has not been controverted by filing any reply to the same. The learned Advocate submitted that sections 69, 73 and 74 of the Town Improvement Act are not attracted in this case. On the other hand, section 40(b) allows alteration or revision of the plan for improvement. 

11. We have perused the petitions, affidavits, as well as the annexures, and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates. The facts of the instant writ petitions are in many respects similar to those in the case report in 7 BLC (AD) 167. In that case, eight plots were developed on the bank of the lake along a 20 ft wide road under similar circumstances. Their Lordships held that: 

"Having considered the facts and circumstances we find that the respondent had no vested legal right to have open space between her house and lake. There is no evidence that the lake has been or is being filled up for the project. The narrow strip of vacant land, which is being converted into plots is only an extension/addition to Gulshan residential plots by altering the layout plan, and would not adversely affect the environment of Gulshan or destroy the greeneries or the lake. There has been no change of the master plan either."

 12. In the instant case also we find that there is no evidence or material with regard to filling up of the lake in anyway. On the contrary, the report of the investigation by the Ministry of Environment shows that the lake has not been filled in. On scrutiny of the original layout plan, it appears that the amenities such as park, playground, school, mosque, etc. are clearly marked in the map itself. The open space in front of Road No. 20 does not appear to have been marked for any such purpose. It appears to us that the benefit of the open space in front of the petitioner's plot was a momentary fortuitous benefit, which has been taken away for the greater benefit of the community at large, which is for the provision of extra plots necessary to meet the demands of the population. 

13. The claim that Road No. 20 was meant for pedestrians use only and that a 20 ft wide road is in violation of section 54 of the Town Improvement Act does not hold good, since it cannot be claimed that Road No. 20 would not be used by the enquiry that Road No. 20 was 20 fit wide. Moreover, we note that there are number of other roads within the vicinity, which are less than the 40 feet wide roads required by law as propounded in section 54 of the Act. In any event, since the petitioners did not complain about the size of the other roads, they cannot now complain that the road is only 20 feet wide. With regard to access of air and cross ventilation, the petitioner and the o residents adjoining her plot are no worse off than the residents on either side of Road No. 20. All the plots are back to back as are the new plots with the petitioner's plot. She has not suffered any greater disadvantage than any of her other neighbours in Uttara. In the instant case, there is no evidence that lake has been reduced in size. On the other hand, the new road will provide a promenade overlooking the lake, which will be for the enjoyment of all the residents in the locality.

 14. The decisions in the case reported in 53 DLR (AD) 79 [same as 11 BLT (AD) 561 and the unreported decision in WP 1046 of 1993 are somewhat different in that in those cases there was a clear finding that land earmarked for park, school, mosque, etc. had been reallocated as residential plots. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, we are satisfied that the land in question was not earmarked for any civic amenity nor was the lake encroached upon. 

15. We find ourselves in complete agreement with the decision of their Lordships in the case reported in 7 BLC (AD) 167 and find no merits in the instant writ petitions, which are liable to be discharged. 

In the result, both the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. 

End.

lawyer:
Abdur Razzaq with Md Hossain, Advocates -For the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000, 1320, 1327, 1328, 1329, 1965 of 2001. 

Mahmudul Islam, Attorney-General with Mahbubey Alam, Additional Attorney-General with Obaidul Hasan Shaheen, Deputy Attorney-General with Probir Neogi, Assistant Attorney-General, with Naima Haider, Assistant Attorney-General with Bhabesh Chandra Sarkar, Assistant Attorney-General -For the Respondents.
parties:
Afzalul Abedin and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
M A Aziz J: The petitioners in all the above 486 Writ petitions have made it their common cause to challenge the Constitutionality of the Public Safety (Special Provision) Act, 2000 (Act VII of 2000) briefly the PSA “জননিরাপত্তা (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০০০”, on the following, amongst other, grounds:

(i) The PSA is inherently prone to arbitrary and discriminatory use.

(ii) Its Provisions are so much overlapping with those of the Penal Code that the law enforcing agencies and the Courts find it difficult to use it properly and judicially.

(iii) It lacks guidelines for the conduct of its exercise thus enabling it to be used and grossly abused by the Government and the Police (Sub-Inspector and Inspectors who are entrusted to record the first information report and investigate the case) to "Pick and Choose" between persons similarly situated and normally liable to be prosecuted under the ordinary law of the land i.e. the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code, briefly CrPC, by arbitrarily and maliciously exposing them to the harsher Provisions of the PSA.

(iv) It is ex facie illegal as it is enacted and used against persons politically opposed to the Ruling Party or, in other words, it is used as a means of selective prosecution.

(v) The Act gives Police the power to make moment-to-moment judgment on his beat.

(vi) It has taken away the jurisdiction of the Court to grant bail within a period of 90 days till Police Report under section 173 CrPC is submitted.

(vii) It denies fair trial and inflicts more severe punishment than under the Penal Code.

(viii) It takes away the inherent power of the High Court Division exercisable under section 561A, the power of revision under section 439 and the power of transfer of cases under section 526 of the CrPC.

(ix) It has introduced a bizarre, alien and outlandish procedure under section 14 to record the statement of a witness under section 164 of the CrPC and to use the same as evidence to corroborate evidence adduced by other witnesses, though it stands on no higher and better footing than a statement made to the Police under section 161 CrPC. And though it can be used only by the accused to contradict the prosecution witnesses and the benefit, if any, is given to the accused, under the PSA the benefits given to the prosecution instead of to the accused which of course is contrary to the rule of law.

(x) It lacks the procedural safeguard and fairness of trial as section 18 of the PSA provides that the tribunal shall try cases summarily in accordance with section 264 of the CrPC: that chapter XX of the Said Code shall as far as practicable be followed and that instead of recording the testimony of the witnesses in full only the substance of the same shall be recorded. Chapter XX of the CrPC speaks of the trial of summons cases by Magistrates while Chapter XXI speaks of trial of warrant cases by Magistrates. The difference and distinction that once existed between summons procedure and warrant procedure have long been done away with. Now there is only one procedure i.e. warrant procedure. Whereas section 264 which comes under Chapter XXII of the CrPC. (of Summary trial) provides that in every case tried summarily by a Magistrate, such Magistrate shall before passing sentence record judgment embodying the substance of the evidence and that such judgment sjiall be the only record in cases coming within this section. While section 260 of the CrPC provides that any first class Magistrate specially empowered by the government if he thinks fit may try in a summary way all or any of the following offences:

(a) Offences not punishable with death, transportation for life (Now imprisonment for life)

(b) …………….

(c) …………….

(d) ……………..

Now that the Tribunal or Adalat under the PSA who is a Sessions Judge records as he is empowered under section 264 CrPC only the substance of the evidence and passes a sentence of imprisonment for life, in appeal as provided under section 24 of the PSA, the convict would be very gravely prejudiced in getting a fair trial because in a criminal appeal unlike that of revision under section 439' CrPC or second Appeal and revision under the CPC the whole matter is laid bare before the appellate Court. He is a court of facts as well as of law and appreciation and evaluation of evidence differs and varies from Judge to Judge more so when only the substances of the evidence instead of the evidence in its entirety comes before the appellate Court. This is an inbuilt mechanism for perpetuation of procedural injustice hitting at the root of the principle of fair trial and the rule of law.

Professor Wade in his Administrative Law (sixth edition) in dealing with procedural justice said "Procedure is not a matter of secondary importance. As governmental powers continually grow more drastic, it is only by procedural fairness that they are rendered tolerable. The legislation which controls the use of land, for example, contains a large element of expropriation without compensation, which is for the most part accepted without pubic complaint. But if there is the least suggestion that planning appeal has been handled unfairly, public complaint is loud and widespread. Mr Frankfurter, a Judge of the United States Supreme Court, said; in the case of Shaughnessy vs United States 345 US (1943) "procedural fairness and regularity are of the indispensable essence of liberty. Severe substantive laws can be endured if they are fairly and impartially applied. He went on to say that it might be preferable to live under Russian Law applied by common law procedures than under the common law enforced by Russian Procedures. One of his colleagues said "The history of liberty has largely been the history of the observance of procedural safeguards."

(xi) Frequently first information reports lodged under the Penal Code are changed/altered by the police to one under the PSA. Exactly this is what happened in Writ Petition No. 76 of 2001, and a host of other Writ petitions. In Writ Petition No. 1274 of 2001 two first information reports were lodged one under the Penal Code and the other one under the PSA on identical facts.

(xii) In writ petitions i.e Writ Petition Nos. 4430 of 2000 and 76 of 2001 (in the latter petition through a supplementary affidavit) the PSA has been challenged to be a fraud on the Constitution, the President, the Parliament and, above all, the people.

(xiii) The extract/Summary of the Bill (PSA) was presented to the President for his recommendation to be introduced into the Parliament as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not as a money Bill as required under Article 82 of the Constitution. And though the President recommended the same as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not as a Money Bill, the Home Minister introduced the Bill into the House telling the legislature that it was recommended by the President as a Money Bill. This is a prevarication and travesty of truth, which is evident from Annexure "5" and "6" respectively of the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 1 (Government).

(xiv) The PSA was passed as a Money Bill though in reality it was not a money Bill in terms of Article 81(1)(a) to (f) and, as such, the Parliament had no power to pass the Bill' as a money bill.

(xv) After the Bill was passed, the Speaker under Article 81(3) gave a certificate that it was a money bill and presented it to the President for his assent that it was a Money Bill though the Speaker had no power to certify the Bill as a Money Bill in the face of Article 81(1) of the Constitution.

Before issuance of the certificate the Speaker must satisfy himself that the Bill was a money Bill. In not doing so and by giving the certificate that the PSA was a Money Bill, the Speaker practiced fraud upon the President by taking away and robbing the President of his constitutional prerogative under Article 80(3) and (4). The Speaker did also transgress Article 7(1) of the Constitution, because "all powers in the Republic belong to the people, and their exercise on behalf of the people shall be affected only under, and by authority, of this Constitution." The PSA not being a Money Bill in terms of Article 81(1) of the Constitution, the Speaker had no power to certify the same to be a Money Bill. More so he is incapacitated to do so because he is oath bound to protect, preserve and defend the Constitution.

(xvi) The Hon'ble President, who was previously the Chief Justice of Bangladesh, by issuing a public statement, which is very uncommon and unusual, denied to have ever recommended the PSA as a money bill for its introduction into the Parliament as a money bill and this is not denied.

2. Upon these assertions all the above Rules were issued on different dates calling upon the respondents (mainly the Government of Bangladesh) to show cause, why the PSA should not be declared to be void being ultra vires the fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 27, 31, 32, and 35 of the Constitution and for violation of Articles 7, 26(2), 65(1), 81(1), 80(3), 101, 109 and 116A of the Constitution.

And of those 25 sections the following are the Penal sections i.e. section 4 hijacking, 5 extortion or collection of subscription, 6 interference with tender, 7 causing damage and destruction to cars and properties, 8 obstruction to the plying of vehicles, 9 demand and realisation of ransom, 10 creating of panic, 11 filing of false cases and section 12 is abetment of offence. 8. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel referred to Annexure "C" to Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000 and submitted that the Bill was presented to the President by the Ministry of Home Affairs through the Prime Minister for the former's recommendation for its introduction into the Parliament as a Bill involving expenditure of public money (item No. 5 of Annexure "C") and not as a money bill. The President accordingly recommended the Bill for its introduction into the Parliament as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not as a Money Bill.

9. The Home Minister notified the Parliament that the Bill would be placed as a Money Bill, stating that the President's recommendation had been obtained to place if as a Money Bill. After the Bill was passed, the Speaker certified that this was a Money Bill (emphasis is mine). The Bill was eventually placed before the President for his assent. The Prime Minister's Press Secretary by a rejoinder published in the Daily Star published on 14-2-2000 & 21-2000 (Annexures-I and I(1) respectively to Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000) maintained that the Bill was a Money Bill within the meaning of Article 81(1)(e) of the Constitution and the President recommended it as a Money Bill before it was introduced into the Parliament.

10. A Press release issued from the President's House publicly denied that the President recommended the PSA as a Money Bill before its introduction into Parliament. It was further explained publicly that the Prime Minister's proposal placed before him (President) for recommendation was for a Bill involving expenditure from public exchequer, but such involvement of public money does not mean that the Bill was a Money Bill. The President's Press release also pointed out that there was a discrepancy between the Bill faxed to the President by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs on 31-1-2000 and the one later on shown to him by the Law Minister and that this had not yet been explained to the President.

11. It is submitted that the PSA was not a Money Bill under Article 81(1) of the Constitution. The Government though asserted in their Affidavit-in-Opposition in Paragraph 7 (Seven) in Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000 that the PSA was a Money Bill and was passed by the Parliament, certificated by the Speaker and assented to by the President as such because it was a Money Bill under Article 81(1)(d) of the Constitution. What is a money bill has been defined in Article 81(1) of the Constitution which runs as follows:

Article 81. Money Bill (1). In this Part "Money Bill" means—

(a) the imposition, regulation, alteration, remission or repeal of any tax;

(b) the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government, or the amendment of any law relating to the financial obligations of the Government;

(c) the custody of the Consolidated Fund, the payment of money into, or the issue or appropriation of moneys from, the Fund;

(d) the imposition of a charge upon the Consolidated Fund or the alteration or abolition of any such charge;

(e) the receipt of moneys on account of the Consolidated Fund or the Public Account of the Republic, or the custody or issue of such moneys, or the audit of the accounts of the Government;

(f) any subordinate matter incidental to any of the matters specified in the foregoing sub-clauses.

12. Mr Ahmed submits that none of the Provisions of the PSA answer to the description enumerated under Article 81(1)(a)-(f) nor is it covered by Article 81(1)(d) because on a reference to Article 88 of the Constitution it is found that only a handful of specified expenditure has been made chargeable upon the Consolidated Fund enumerated hereunder:

Article 88. Charges on Consolidated Fund. The following expenditure shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund—

(a) the remuneration payable to the President and other expenditure relating to his officer;

(b) the remuneration payable to—

(i) the Speaker and Deputy Speaker;

(ii) the Judges of the [Supreme Court]:

(iii) the Comptroller and Auditor-General;

(iv) the Election Commissioners;

(v) the members of the Public Service Commission;

(c) the administrative expenses of, including remuneration payable to, officers and servants of Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Comptroller and Auditor General, the Election Commission and the Public Service Commissions;

(d) all debt charges for which the Government is liable, including interest, sinking fund charges, the repayment of amortisation of capital, and other expenditure in connection with the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt;

(e) any sums required to satisfy a judgment, decree or award against the Republic by any court or tribunal; and

(f) any other expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund by this Constitution or by Act of Parliament.

Furthermore Article 81(2) provides as follows:

(2) A Bill shall not be deemed to be a Money Bill by reason only that it provides for the imposition or alteration of any fine or other pecuniary penalty, or for the levy or payment of a licence fee or a fee or charge for any service rendered, or by reason only that it provides for the imposition, regulation, alteration, remission or repeal of any tax by a local authority or body for local purposes.

13. In the case of Dira Dockyard and Engineers Ltd and others vs Shilpa Rin Sangstha and others 39 DLR (AD) 59 it was held that when the word "means" is used (in Article 81 of the Constitution the word means has been used in defining Money Bill saying "Money Bill" means:) in any clause or section it puts a limit, nothing more being in contemplation; but if the word "includes" is used it means something more than what is in terms specified. The use of the word "includes" does not exclude other possible meanings besides that have been expressly mentioned in the clause" and hence the definition of Money Bill is exhaustive. To counter this hurdle, the learned Attorney-General Mr Mahmudul Islam, argued that many such or similar Bills were passed and assented to by the President as Money Bills in the past by various governments and as such it has become a parliamentary practice. This was answered to by Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed saying "such illegal and unconstitutional practice or precedent cannot be used as a justification for the present Bill being described as a Money Bill when it does not answer the description of Article 81(1) of the Constitution. I find tremendous force and substance in this argument and do accept it. There can be no estoppel against a statute and more so against the supreme law of the land which is the solemn expression of the will of the people i.e. the Constitution.

14. The next argument advanced by the learned Counsel is that the PSA is a colorable legislation and, as such, a fraud on the Constitution inasmuch as the Parliament had no competence to pass such a Bill as a Money Bill.

15. Under Article 65(1) the legislative power vested in the Parliament is in the following term "here shall be a parliament for Bangladesh (to be known as the House of the Nation) in which subject to the Provisions of this Constitution, shall be vested the legislative Powers of the Republic. So, the lawmaking power of the Parliament is a limited one because where the Constitution as ours is supreme and the legislature is a creature of the Constitution with limitations on its competence, its laws being liable to be struck down as ultra vires if they preach the constitutional controls, it is called a "controlled constitution". In such a constitution the legislature's power to alter the constitution is non existent.

16. Every constitutionally trained mind will instantly click on and envision the Parliament at Westminster the moment it is said that the Parliament is supreme. The British Parliament has the plenary power to enact law. This power is uncontrolled, unfettered and unrestrained. No Court in Great Britain can refuse to enforce any Act of Parliament let alone declaring it ultra vires or unconstitutional. They, however, have the power to interpret the law and in so doing they have the power to remove elements unjust and unreasonable in the Statute upon the presumption of the Parliament's lack of intention of prescribing anything unreasonable and arbitrary. But ours is a written and rigid Constitution like those of the United States of America, India, Pakistan, Japan, Singapore, and others. Our Parliament is on and under a constitutional leash and circumspection. Here it is the Constitution and not the Parliament which is supreme.

17. In the third paragraph of the preamble of our Constitution it has been pledged that it shall be the fundamental aim of the, state to realise through a democratic process a socialist society, free from exploitation, a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social, will be secured for all citizens.

18. In the fourth paragraph it has been affirmed that it is our sacred duty to safeguard, protect and defend our Constitution and to maintain its supremacy as the embodiment of the will of the people of Bangladesh.

19. Few constitutions do have such a preamble as ours. In the words of Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed it stands like the "Statue of Liberty" and shines like the "Pole Star". There is no scope for debate whether it does or does not form part of the Constitution as has been the case in some countries. It is not only an integral part of the Constitution. It is so deeply and strongly rooted and entrenched in the Constitution that even under Article 142, the Parliament is powerless to amend it by way of addition, alteration, substitution or repeal. It can be amended by the people alone in a referendum as it has proceeded from the people and it is not just a rhetorical flourish. We have achieved our Constitution after a gloriously successful War of Independence.

20. Article 7(1) Postulates the supremacy of the Constitution. It ordains that all powers in the Republic belong to the people and their exercise on behalf of the people shall be effected only under and by authority of, this Constitution.

<u>21. Article 7(2) enjoins that this Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. So, the Parliament must have the power to make a particular law which of course includes procedures i.e. the mechanism through which it is implemented. It is submitted that the PSA is a colorable legislation because Parliament has sought to enact it as a Money Bill which it could never have enacted under Article 81(1) of the Constitution. Being colourable such a legislation is void.</u>

<u>22. The learned Attorney-General disputes this proposition stating that the concept of colourable legislation is relatable only to a Federal System of Government where the Federal and Provincial legislatures encroach upon one another's domain in law making. Mr Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that this is not the universal rule. It may occur and did occur in this country and cited the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319. In that case the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Re-organisation) (Repeal) Ordinance, 1991 was challenged. By that Ordinance Upazila Parishads were abolished but the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished Parishads were vested in the Government. Article 59 of the Constitution provides that local government in any administrative unit of the Republic shall be entrusted to bodies composed of persons elected in accordance with law. It was challenged as a colourable legislation because by vesting the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished parishads in the government, indirectly local government functions of the Upazila Parishad were sought to be entrusted to persons who were not elected by the people, result being that in form it is a Repeal Act, but in substance it continued the Upazila Parishads and vested the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the Parishads in the Government. Article 59 requires that the Upazila Parishad shall be composed of elected persons and Article 60 requires the Parliament to confer necessary powers including the power to impose taxes for local purposes upon the local bodies, but the Repeal Act, in the guise of abolition of the Parishads, has, in fact, retained them so that their functions can be performed by government through their officers. Their Lordships held that "if this contention is correct and the Upazila Parishads are still functioning through government officers, then the Act will not only be colourable legislation, but it will be a fraud on the Constitution, in which case we shall have no hesitation to declare it void."</u>

<u>The question of colourable legislation arises when a thing which cannot be done directly is sought to be done indirectly. A thing is colourable which exists in appearance and not in reality. It is "what it purports to be” Colourability is linked up with incompetence, that is, an authority doing a thing which he got no power to do. "Colourable" is not tainted with bad faith; it is just lack of law-making power. The doctrine of colourable legislation does not involve any question of bonafide on the part of the legislature. If the legislature is competent to pass a particular law, the motives which impelled it to act are really irrelevant. As stated in Cooley's Constitutional Limitation, "whether a statute is constitutional or not is always a question of power. The learned Attorney-General has in this connection referred to a ,few Indian cases including KCG Narayan Deo vs State of Orissa, AIR 1953 SC 379.</u>

<u>In Modern Constitutions State powers are distributed among the three Organs or Departments of Government. Legislature is one of the three organs. It is assigned the legislative powers which are clearly demarcated and it has to act within its own field and cannot transgress the limits set by the Constitutional provisions. If the Legislature transgresses the limits, it may be stopped and the transgression may be declared a nullity by the Judiciary—another State Organ. The transgression may be "patent, manifest or direct"; it may also be "disguised, covert and indirect". This latter class of transgression is expressed as colourable legislation in judicial pronouncements. Elaborating this doctrine Duff-J made the following observation in Attorney-General for Ontario vs Reciprocal Insurers, 1924 AC 328;</u>

<u>"Where the law making authority is of a limited or qualified character it may he necessary to examine with some strictness the substance of the legislation for the purpose of determining what is that the legislature is really doing."</u>

<u>It is, therefore, the substance of a law and not its form that matters. If the subject matter of a law in substance is something which is beyond the Legislature's power to legislate upon, its outward form cannot save it from the mischief of judicial review. In such cases investigation may be held to find out whether what has been made is, in fact, within the power of the Legislature. For the purpose of this investigation, Court can examine the effect of the legislation and take into consideration its object, purpose and design. (Attorney-General for Alberta vs Attorney-General for Canada, 1939 AC 117.</u>

23. The appeal in Kudrat-e-Elahi's case was however dismissed on the technical ground that Article 9 postulating promotion of local government institutions and falling under the Fundamental Principles of State Policy cannot be judicially enforceable and the Upazila Parishad was not a local body. In that case Shahabuddin Ahmed, CJ observed; "It appears to us that the words rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished Parishad have apparently created an impression that those attributes of the Parishad have remained to be enjoyed by the Government, If these words are deleted then no confusion is left". Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh observed at page 306 (4.29) that when legislature uses certain words in the law, the question of deletion of those words is a matter for consideration of the legislature and not of the court. If those words create unconstitutionality, the words should be declared ultra vires, provided those words are severable, otherwise the whole law is to be declared ultra vires.

24. In reply to Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed's contention that the PSA is a colourable legislation because had it not been under the guise of a Money Bill the Parliament could never have enacted it as it did not have the power to do so and the PSA was never a Money Bill, the learned Attorney-General argued that the constitutional validity of the law cannot be questioned, because of the embargo under Article 78(1) and Article 81(3) of the Constitution and because the concept of colourable legislation is relatable to the competence of the legislature rather than to any question of malafide or fraud.

25. Mr Ahmed argued that what has been impugned is the law itself on three grounds, namely, its being void as a colourable legislation, its being void as having contravened fundamental rights under Articles 27, 31, 32 and 33 of the Constitution and for its having taken away the inherent power of the Courts. He further submits that the English decisions cited by the learned Attorney-General i.e. Bradlaugh vs Gosset 12 QBD 271, British Railway Board vs Pickin (1974) AC 765, Edinburgh and Dalkeith Railway Co vs Wanchope (1842) 8 CL & F 710), Labrado Co vs Queen (1893) AC 104, Hoani Te Heuthen Tukino vs Aotca District Maori Land Board (194) AC 308 are precedents on immunity of Parliamentary Proceedings. Everybody knows, (Lord Denning however had something to say as regards clauses ousting the jurisdiction of courts in his famous book, "The Discipline of Law" to which I shall devote some paragraphs at an appropriate stage) about the principle of immunity of Parliamentary Proceedings in Britain. But we must not lose sight of the reality that in England unlike Bangladesh the Courts do not have the power or jurisdiction to review a legislative act. The Courts in England interpret and apply the law. Thus the precedents on Parliamentary Privilege cited by the learned Attorney-General are totally unnecessary and need not be gone into. I am in full agreement with Mr Ahmed on this point.

26. In our country as has been said earlier, the Parliament is not supreme rather it is the Constitution which is supreme. The Parliament is a creature of the Constitution. As such if the Proceedings of the Parliament are outside the purview or are contrary to any provision of the Constitution, it would not qualify as a Proceeding in Parliament and, the court's jurisdiction is not ousted. The law passed in a sitting of Parliament when there was no quorum, such a sitting will not qualify as a lawful Proceeding of Parliament. If total strangers of intruders have, without any colour of title of membership, participated in a proceeding, such a proceeding will not be valid and the courts can adjudicate on the validity of such proceeding.

27. The immunity extends to the formal transaction of the business of Parliament, and whatever is not related to such transaction is not covered by the immunity thus, a question relating to the title of a person to be a member of Parliament or to continue to sit therein is a question relating to the transaction of the business of Parliament, and the courts are not precluded from questioning or considering this matter because of the embargo placed under Article 78(1) of the Constitution as proposed by the learned Attorney-General. Mr Ahmed has quoted para 4.86 from the Constitutional Law of Bangladesh by Mr Mahmudul Islam on the privileges of members and officers of Parliament as follows:

4.86 Privileges of members and officers: The members and officers of Parliament are not amenable to the jurisdiction of court in respect of acts done by them in exercise of powers granted to them by the Constitution or by law including the rules of procedure of Parliament to regulate the procedure in Parliament or to conduct the business of Parliament or to maintain order in Parliament. The court will not interfere with the functioning of the Speaker inside Parliament in the matter of regulation of the conduct of business of Parliament. The Speaker cannot be sued for damages for wrongful arrest of a person under Warrant issued by him on charge of contempt of the legislature as the Speaker in issuing the warrant was acting in performance of his duties connected with the internal affairs of the legislature. In Bradlaugh vs Gossett the plaintiff’s action against a Sergeant-at-Arms, who ejected the plaintiff, a member of the House of Commons, from the House of Commons was dismissed on the ground that the Sergeant-at-Arms was acting under a resolution of the House of Commons and was protected.

28. The PSA is questioned, he submits, not because there has been any fraud in the Proceedings of Parliament or the Bill was void because it was fraudulently introduced in Parliament. It is questioned on the ground of its being a colourable legislation inasmuch as it was a law made by the Parliament when it was not competent to pass the Act as a Money Bill under the Constitution. Article 81(1) and the Parliament had indirectly done something which it could not have done directly. The issue or colourable legislation has earlier been dealt with in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh in detail.

29. As to the bar of or the ouster of jurisdiction of courts provided under Article 78(1) of the Constitution i.e. "the Proceedings in Parliament shall not be questioned in any court," the learned Attorney-General cited a host of English decision including Bradlaugh vs Gosset, British Railway Board vs Pickin, Edinburgh and Dalkeith Railway Co vs Wanchope, Labrado Co vs The Queen and Mr Ishtiaq Ahmed did not dispute the principle enunciated and upheld in those cases but he contended that those cases are clearly distinguishable from the cases we are grappling with because there is hardly any scope to think that our Parliament and the Parliament at Westminster are co-equal. Our Parliament as has been said before is a creature of the Constitution and it is not the Parliament rather the Constitution which is supreme and that being so the cases referred to above are of no avail. They do not in any manner support the learned Attorney-General. The learned Counsel for the petitioner cited the case of Farzand Ali vs Province of West Pakistan PLD 1970 SC 98 in which Hamoodur Rahman CJ said "I have carefully examined the cases relied upon in the High Court and the learned Counsel for the respondents in these appeals but I have not come across any case in which the question arose in the precise form in which it has arisen in the present case. The elaborate discussion in the judgment of this court in Ahmad Saeed Kirmani's case given by Cornelius, J., as his Lordship then was, with regard to the lea- et consuetude Parliament compelled him also to come to the conclusion that the only point on which there was unanimity in the English Courts was that matters which can fairly be described as internal proceedings relating to the proper business of the House are wholly outside the corrective jurisdiction of the High Court." He too however, noticed that with regard to the Privileges of the House there was no immunity in the English Courts and Denman, CJ, in Burdett's cases (1811)14 East 1, did assert the right of the courts to decide whether a claim of privilege was within the jurisdiction of the House claiming it.

30. In the case of Bradlaugh vs Gosset QBD (DB) 273 all that was conceded was that "what is said or done within the walls of Parliament cannot be enquired into in a court of law." The jurisdiction of the House, said Lord Coledridge CJ, "over their own members, their rights to impose discipline within their walls is absolute and exclusive."

31. Stephen J, in the same case quoted with approval the observation of Coleridge J., in the case of Stockdale vs Hawsurd 8 (AD) & El 114, to the effect that "the House should have exclusive jurisdiction to regulate the course of its own proceedings, and animadvert upon any conduct there in violation of its rules or derogation from its dignity, stands upon the clearest of necessity."

32. But the Parliament cannot claim any immunity if it transgresses or oversteps its limits under the Constitution which it did in passing a non-Money Bill as a Money Bill and hence Article 78(1) cannot preclude or debar the courts from exercising their power of judicial review of the unconstitutional acts.

33. It was argued that the PSA though was not a Money Bill yet it was passed as a Money Bill under Article 81(1) of the Constitution and the certificate issued by the Speaker under Article 81(3) of the Constitution was a fraud practised by the Speaker upon the Constitution, the President, the Parliament and, above all, the people of Bangladesh who granted the power of certificate to the Speaker and hence the PSA is ultra wires the Constitution and as such void.

34. To repulse this aggressive contention the learned Attorney-General tried to use Article 81(3) of the Constitution that the certificate issued by the Speaker that it is a Money Bill shall be conclusive for all purposes and shall not be questioned in any court as a shield or in other words, he contended that the aforesaid Article provides a blanket coverage against the power of courts in its exercise of judicial review.

35. The expression "Certificate" has not been defined in the Constitution. In Black's Law Dictionary (6th Edition) it has been defined "as a written assurance, or official representation, that some act has or has not been done, or some event occurred, or some legal formality has been complied with. A written assurance made or issued from some court, and designed as a notice of things done therein, or as a warrant or authority, to some other court, judge, or officer. A statement of some fact in a writing signed by the party certifying a declaration in writing. A "Certificate" by a public officer is a statement written and signed, but not necessarily sworn to, which is by law made evidence of the truth of the facts stated for all or for certain purposes. A document certifying that one has fulfilled the requirements of and may practice in a field."

36. In P Ramanatha Aiyar's Law Lexicon (1997 Edition) "Certificate" has been defined as "A writing by which an officer or other person bears testimony that a fact has or has not taken place' as written testimony to the truth of any fact (Webster); a writing so signed and authenticated as to be legal evidence; a writing by which testimony is given that a fact has or has not taken place. A 'Certificate', ex vi termini, imports that the party certifying knows the fact that he certifies." Per Kenyon CJ, Farmer vs Legg. 7 TR 191.

37. Now that "Certificate", according to Black and P Rahmanatha" being a written testimony to the truth of any fact "and according to Article 81(3) of the Constitution every money Bill shall, when it is presented to the President for his assent, bear as certificate under the hand of the Speaker "that" it is a "Money Bill" convey in the clearest of term that before such a certificate is issued the Speaker must "satisfy" himself that what he is certifying is a money Bill and a Money Bill alone, reason being two-fold firstly, this is a constitutional power granted to him by the people to be exercised on behalf of the people and shall be effected only under, and by authority of the Constitution (Article 7(1) of the Constitution) and secondly, because the grant of power under Article 81(3) of the Constitution itself has placed a condition or an embargo upon such power by employing the expression "that" the Bill shall bear a certificate under the hand of the Speaker "that" it is a Money Bill. As such, it is not an open-handed licence rather the power to exercise this grant of power is qualified and hedged with a condition which of necessity is required to be fulfilled as a condition precedent before the power can be exercised. It is so, because this extraordinary power is granted to the Speaker only as a means of ''shortening the process" of passing a Bill without the rigours of discussion in the parliamentary standing committee and the first, second and third reading of the Bill in the House of Parliament and this is necessary because on occasions the Government may need to raise money immediately by way of imposition of tax or levy -or by borrowing and the normal and usual practice may frustrate the very purpose. Furthermore, by this exercise of power by the Speaker, the President is denied, denuded and robbed of his constitutional prerogative granted to him under Article 80(3) of the Constitution. This is permissible only when the concerned Bill is a Money Bill and Money Bill alone. The Speaker's certificate is not at all necessary if the Bill is not a Money Bill according to Article 81(1) of the Constitution. If the Bill is other than a Money Bill the President under sub-Article (3) of Article 80 of the Constitution may return it to Parliament with a message requesting that the Bill or any particular provisions thereof be reconsidered, and that any amendments specified by him in the message be considered. Under sub-Article 4 of Article 80 as aforesaid if the Bill is so returned the Parliament shall consider the same together with the President's message and if the Bill is again passed by Parliament with or without amendments [by the votes of a majority of the total number of members of Parliament] as pointed out by Mr Abdur Razzaq, learned Counsel appearing in Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000. He argued that once such a Bill is returned by the President under Article 80(3) of the Constitution, the Parliament though may pass the Bill again with or without amendments shall have to consider it together with the President's message and this requirement is not an idle exercise inasmuch as sub-Article (4) of Article 80 of the Constitution enjoins that if the President so returns the Bill, Parliament shall consider it together with the President's message (emphasis is mine) and such a Bill can be passed by Parliament (with or without amendments) by the votes of a majority of the total number of members of Parliament. Normally a Bill may be passed by the vote of the majority of members present. But according to sub-Article (2) of Article 75 of the Constitution, only 60 (sixty) members do form a quorum. Therefore, a Bill may be passed by a majority of those sixty members present. Whereas, if a Bill is returned to the Parliament for reconsideration (when it is a Bill other than a Money Bill as is the case before us) it can only be passed by the votes of a majority of the total number of members of Parliament as provided under Article 80(4) of the Constitution and Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure meaning thereby that of the 330 members a minimum of 166 members are required to pass a Bill returned by the President. A money Bill as we have seen under Article 80(3) of the Constitution that the President has no power to return to the Parliament for reconsideration.

38. None of the provisions of the PSA which I have very carefully scanned through does attract the mischief of Money Bill defined under Article 81(1) of the Constitution. Even then the Speaker issued a certificate saying that it was a Money Bill thus overstepping and transgressing Article 81(1) and 81(3) respectively of the Constitution. 55. The function of the court in interpreting any provision of a Constitution is to ascertain the intention of the makers of the Constitution. This is the pole star in the construction of the Constitution and all other principles are only rules or guides to aid in the determination of that intention. As the language primarily expresses the intention, effort should be made at the first instance to gather it from the words used and upon consideration of the whole of the enactment. A clause cannot be interpreted in isolation and must be construed as part of a unified whole. "The legal intendment is that each and every clause has been inserted for some useful purpose, and, when rightfully understood has some practical operation; each word, it has been said, must be presumed to have been carefully chosen and intentionally placed, as though it had been hammered into place." Every word must be given effect to and no word as a general rule should be rendered meaningless or inoperative. The court must lean in favour of a construction which will render every word operative rather than that which makes some words idle or nugatory. When the same expression is used in several places, it has to be construed as meaning the same thing unless the context otherwise requires. In the same way if different words are used, they must be understood as conveying different meanings. Though in popular sense the expressions 'dismissal' and 'removal from service' have the same meaning, but different expressions having been used, the same meaning to both terms was not given. In ascertaining the intention it is wrong to start with some a priori idea of that intention and then to try by interpretation to wedge into the words of the Constitution. If the language of the Constitution is not only plain, but admits of only one meaning, the language declares the intention even if the result is harsh. In such a case the court is not at liberty to search for a meaning beyond the instrument. But when a provision apparently within the competence of the legislature to make it appears to be unduly harsh or absurd, the court is put to enquiry whether the framers of the Constitution intended to confer such power of the legislature. This is particularly so when the concept of reasonable law is embedded in the fabric of the Constitution as the case of the American and the Bangladesh Constitutions. It will be seen that generally the court defers to the legislative judgment regarding reasonableness of a law, but when a statute was found to be quite unreasonable and unnecessarily impinging on the accepted values of the society, the American Supreme Court declared such law void as not being permitted by the Constitution.

It is a judge made rule (Bangladesh Constitution is to a great extent specific because Articles 7 and 102 read together confer this power to the judges of the higher court). In 1908 Charles Evans Hughes the tenth Chief Justice firmly declared, "we are under the Constitution, but the Constitution is what the judges say it is and the judiciary is the safeguard of our liberty and our property under the Constitution. The American Constitution nowhere provides that it shall be what the judges say it is. Yet it has become the most fundamental and far reaching principle of American constitutional law."

One Law Lord held that the tribunal made no error of law at all.

58. So, we are left with a question which no one can expect to answer rightly. Is it not then time to go back to the starting point? And to ask: were the courts right in the beginning to draw the distinction between within and without jurisdiction"? His Lordship further observed that so fine is the distinction that in truth the High Court has a choice before it whether to interfere with an inferior court on a point of law. If it chooses to interfere, it can formulate its decision in the words: 'The Court below had no jurisdiction to decide this point wrongly as it did". If it does not choose to interfere, it can say: "The court had jurisdiction to decide it wrongly, and did so". Softly be it stated, but that is the reason for the difference between the decision of the Court of Appeal in Anisminic and the House of Lords.

59. I would suggest, said his Lordship, that this distinction should now be discarded. The High Court has, and should have, jurisdiction to control the proceedings of inferior courts and tribunals by way of judicial review. When they go wrong in law, the High Court should have power to put them right not only in the instant case to do justice to the complainant, but also as to secure that all courts and tribunals, when faced with the same point of law, should depend on which judge tries his case, or in what court it is heard. The way to get things right is to hold thus; no court or tribunal has any jurisdiction to make an error of law on which the decision of the case depends. If it makes such an error, it goes outside its jurisdiction and certiorari will lie to correct it. In saying this, however, I should make it clear that I am making a distinction between "Judicial power" and "Jurisdiction." In a system where there is a trichotomy of sovereign powers, then ex necessitate rei from the very nature of things the judicial power must be vested in the judiciary. But what is this judicial power. "Judicial Power" has been defined in the Corpus Juris Secundum, Vol XVI, Paragraph 144, as follows:

"The judiciary or judicial department is an independent and equal coordinate branch of Government, and is that branch thereof which is intended to interpret, construe, and apply the law, or that department of Government which is charged with the declaration of what the law is, and its construction, so far as it is written law.

"This power, it is said, is inherent in the judiciary by reason of the system of division of powers itself under which, as Chief Justice Marshal put it, ''the Legislature makes, the executive execute and the judiciary construe, the Law." Thus, the determination of what the existing law is in relation to something already done or happened is the function of the judiciary while the predetermination of what the law shall be for the regulation of all future cases falling under its provisions is the function of the Legislature.

"It may well be asked at this stage as to what is meant by "jurisdiction"? How does it differ from "judicial power"? Apart from setting up the organs, the Constitution may well provide for a great many other things, such as, the subjects in respect of which that power may be exercised and the manner of the exercise of the power. Thus it may provide that the Courts set up will exercise revisional or appellate powers or only act as a Court of a cessation or only decide Constitutional issues. It may demarcate the territories in which a particular Court shall function and over which its Writs shall run. It may specify the persons in respect of whom the judicial power to hear and determine will be execrable. These are all matters which are commonly comprised in what is called the jurisdiction of the Court. It expresses the concept of the particular res or subject matter over which the judicial power is to be exercised and the manner of its exercise. Jurisdiction is, therefore, a right to adjudicate concerning a particular subject matter in a given case as also the authority to exercise in a particular manner the judicial power vested in the Court.

"In exercising this power, the judiciary claims no supremacy over other organs of the Government but acts only as the administrator of the public will. Even when it declares a legislative measure unconstitutional and void, it does not do so, because, the judicial power is superior in degree or dignity to the legislative power, but because the Constitution has vested it with the power to declare what the law is in the cases which come before it. It thus merely enforces the Constitution as a paramount law whenever a legislative enactment comes into conflict with it because; it is its duty to see that the Constitution prevails. It is only when the Legislature fails to keep within its own Constitutional limits; the judiciary steps in to enforce compliance with the Constitution. This is, no doubt, a delicate task as pointed out in the case of AK Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs Shah Nawaz, which has to be performed with great circumspection but it has nevertheless to be performed as a sacred Constitutional duty when other State functionaries disregard the limitations imposed upon them or claim to exercise power which the people have been careful to withhold from them.

Having gone through the above provision, I for one could not unearth any guideline, rather I find that the so-called guideline is impermissible, imprecise and vague as argued by Dr Kamal Hossain and I agree with him on this point. 70. If the legislature undertakes to define by statute a new offence and to provide for its punishment, it should express its will in language that will not deceive the common mind, every man being entitled to know that certainty when he has committed a crime. In support of this contention Dr Kamal Hossain referred to a case from the American jurisdiction i.e. 92 US 214 United States vs Reese ET Al. In that case the Supreme Court held that "it would be dangerous if the legislature could set a net large enough to catch all possible offenders, and leave it to the courts to step inside and say who could be rightfully detained, and who should be set at large. This would, to some extent, substitute the judicial for the legislative department of the government. The Courts enforce the legislative will when ascertained, if within the constitutional grant of power. Within its legitimate sphere, congress is supreme, and beyond the control of the courts; but if it steps outside of its Constitutional limitations, and attempts that which is beyond its reach, the courts are authorised to, and when called upon in due course of legal proceedings, must, annul its encroachments upon the reserved power of the States and the People."

71. The learned Attorney-General argued that if the law does not lay down any guideline in conferring discretion, generally the law will be bad. But if such policy or guideline (emphasis is mine) can be found in the law and the executive exercises the discretion in violation of the policy or guideline, the executive action rather than the law shall be declared unconstitutional. But in the PSA as I have said there is no guideline to be gathered either from the preamble or from under section 3 of the Act. The contention of the learned Attorney-General is thus of no assistance to him. About guideline provided in the preamble I shall later on dwell on with reference to the Special Courts Bill 1978 dated-1-12-78 AIR 1979 SC 478 referred to by Mr Abdur Razzaq. Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh said:

"The preamble of a statute throws light as to what the statute intends to reach and it has been clearly permissible to have recourse to it as an aid to construing the enacted provisions of the statute. But as it is not recognised as apart of the Act on the ground that it is not enacted in the same way the substantive parts of a statute are enacted, it cannot be used to qualify or cut down the statute if the statute is clear and unambiguous. If, however, the language of the statute is not clear and the words used therein are vague or equivocal, then the meaning which comports with the preamble is to be preferred. The same view is sought to be taken about the preamble of a Constitution. It is said that the preamble is neither a source of power, nor a limitation on the enacting provisions of a Constitution and it cannot be used to modify the language of the Constitution if it is clear, plain and unambiguous giving one and only one meaning. If, however, the language is not clear and the words used therein indicate or are capable of bearing more than one meaning then the meaning which is nearest to the purpose of the Constitution is to be preferred. If the enacting part of the Constitution is ambiguous or open to doubt, the preamble may be referred to resolve the ambiguity or doubt, as it is a good means of finding out the meaning. But an ambiguity or doubt must not be created or imagined in order to bring in the aid of the preamble.

"The position of the preamble of the Constitution of Bangladesh is somewhat different and it should not be, it is submitted, likened to the preamble of a statute. The preamble is a part of our Constitution and cannot be amended without a referendum. The framers of the Constitution took pains to state clearly the philosophy, aims and objectives of the Constitution and to describe the qualitative aspects of the polity the Constitution is designed to achieve. In this situation, the preamble of the Constitution, in its role, cannot be relegated to the position of the preamble of a statute. However, clear a provision of the Constitution may be, if it is found that the plain meaning of the provision runs counter to the spirit and objectives of the Constitution as stated in the preamble, the question should immediately be asked whether the framers of the Constitution intended to bring about the result which the literal construction produces and the court should search for a meaning in conformity with the spirit and objectives of the Constitution as indicated in the preamble because the substantive provisions have been made to achieve the objects and purposes stated in the preamble. It does not, however, mean that the court can stretch the meaning of the preamble so as to receive support for an interpretation the court wants to give. In Registrar, University of Dacca vs Sajjad Hussain 34 DLR (AD) 1 the majority judgment of the Appellate Division referred to the "historic struggle for national liberation' mentioned in the preamble and construed it as being one phase of the continuing struggle after liberation and for such a construction analogy was drawn from communist political philosophy. It is submitted that the qualifying words 'for national liberation' restricted the expanse of the 'historic struggle' which ended with national independence and cannot be comprehended as continuing after the achievement of independence. Furthermore, the Constitution of Bangladesh clearly envisages traditional democratic process and its language cannot be construed with reference to a radically different political philosophy merely because of the use of the words 'socialist society' in the preamble. This brings us to the expression 'socialism' and 'socialist society' used in the preamble. Apparently, these expressions are vague, but the vagueness disappears when we pay attention to the fact that the framers not only used these expressions but also stated the mode of achieving it by using the expression 'through democratic process' and providing in the substantive part of the Constitution a 18th Century tripartite form of government. Read in the proper perspective, there remains no doubt that the framers did not allude to the communist philosophy of State organisation, but conceived of a democratically-run welfare State to eliminate inequality of income and status and standards of life, and to provide a decent standard of living to the working mass of the country. The preamble speaks of 'equality and justice, political, economic and social.' This brings in the concept of distributive justice which aims at removal of economic inequalities and the undoing of injustice resulting from transactions and dealings between unequal’s in the society. This becomes further clear if we refer to Articles. 14 and 19 of the Constitution. The preamble also speaks of the supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law and fundamental human right which will be dealt with separately".

72. In the Special Courts Bill 1978 dated 1-12-78 AIR 1979 SC 478 the question referred to by the president to the Supreme Court under Article 143(1) (Article 106 is the corresponding Article in our Constitution) was : "Whether the Bill or any of the provisions thereof, if enacted, would be constitutionally valid. Annexed to the order of reference was a copy of the Bill which ran as follows:

"The Special Court Bill, 1978.

A Bill to provide for the trial of a certain class of offences"

"Whereas Commissions of Enquiry appointed under the Commissions of Enquiry Act, 1952 have rendered reports disclosing the existence of prima facie evidence of offences committed by persons who have held high public or political offences in the country and others connected with the commission of such offences during the operating of the Proclamation of Emergency dated 25th June, 1975, and during the preceding period commencing 27th Feb., 1975 when it became apparent that offenders were being screened by those whose duty it was to bring them to book;

And Whereas investigations conducted by the Government through its agencies have also disclosed similar offences committed during the period aforesaid;

And Whereas the offences referred to in the recitals aforesaid were committed or continued during the operation of the Promulgation of Emergency dated 25th June, 1975, during which a grave emergency was clamped on the whole country, civil liberties were withdrawn to a great extent, important fundamental rights of the people were suspended, strict censorship on the press was placed and judicial powers were crippled to a large extent;

And whereas it is the constitutional, legal and moral obligation of the State to prosecute persons, involved in the said offences;

And Whereas the ordinary criminal courts due to congestion of work and other reasons cannot reasonably be expected to bring those prosecutions to a speedy termination;

And Whereas it is imperative for the functioning of parliamentary democracy and the institutions created by or under the Constitution of India that the commission of offences referred to in the recitals aforesaid should be judicially determined with the utmost dispatch;

And whereas it is necessary for the said purpose to create additional courts presided over by a sitting Judge of a High Court in India or a person who has held office as a Judge of a High Court in India.

And Whereas it is expedient to make some procedural changes whereby avoidable delay in the final determination of the guilt or innocence of the persons to be tried is eliminated without interfering with the right to a fair trial;

Be it enacted by Parliament in the Twenty-ninth year of the Republic of India as follows:

1. (1) This Act may be called the Special Courts Act, 1978. (2) It shall come into force at once.

2. The Central Government shall by notification create adequate number of courts to be called Special Courts.

3. A Special Court shall take cognisance of or try such cases as are instituted before it or transferred to it as hereinafter provided.

4. (1) If the Central Government is of the opinion that there is prima facie evidence of the commission of an offence alleged to have been committed during the period mentioned in the preamble by a person who held high public or political office in India and that in accordance with the guidelines contained in the preamble hereto said offence ought to be dealt with under the Act, the Central Government shall make a declaration to that effect in every case in which it is of the aforesaid opinion. (2) such declaration shall not be called in question in any court.

5. On such declaration being made any prosecution in respect of such offence shall be instituted only in a Special Court designated by the Central Government and any prosecution in respect of such offence pending in any court in India shall stand transferred to a Special Court designated by the Central Government.

<u>6. If at the date of the declaration in respect of any offence an appeal or revision against any judgment or order in a prosecution in respect of such of, is itself pending in any court of appeal or revision, the same shall stand transferred for disposal of the Supreme Court of India.</u>

7. A Special Court shall be presided over by a sitting Judge of a High Court in India or a person who has held office as a Judge of a High Court in India and nominated by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

8. A Special Court shall have jurisdiction to try any person concerned in the offence in respect of which a declaration is made under section 4 either as principal, conspirator or abettor and all other offences and accused persons as can be jointly tried therewith at one trial in accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

9. A Special Court shall in the trial of such case follow the procedure prescribed by the said Code for the trial of warrant cases before a Magistrate and save as otherwise provided in this Act be governed by the said Code.

10. (1) Notwithstanding anything in the said Code, an appeal shall lie as of right from any judgment or order of a Special Court to the Supreme Court of India both on fact and on law. (2) Except as aforesaid, no appeal or revision shall lie to any court from any judgment or order of a Special Court."

"that the provisions of the Bill and the recitals of the preamble provide sufficient and definite guidance for making the requisite declaration for deciding who should be sent up for trial to the Special Courts; that, in the context, the Bill does not vest arbitrary or uncanalised power in the Government to pick and choose persons for being tried by special Courts; that the procedure prescribed by the Bill for trial before the Special Courts, far from being more onerous than the ordinary procedure, is in certain important respects more beneficial to the accused; and since, in any event, the procedure of the Special Courts is not more onerous than the ordinary procedure, the provisions of the Bill involve no discrimination violative of Article 14.

The recital of the 6th paragraph of the preamble shows the true nexus between the basis of classification under clause 4(1) and the object of the Bill. That paragraph says that it is imperative for the functioning of the Parliamentary democracy and the institutions created by or under the Constitution of India that the commission of offences referred to in the preamble should be judicially determined with the utmost dispatch. If it be true, and we have to assume it to be true, that offences were committed by persons holding high public or political offices in India under cover of the declaration of emergency and in the name of democracy, there can be no doubt that the trial of such persons must be concluded with the utmost dispatch in the interest of the functioning of democracy in our country and the institutions created by our Constitution. Longer these trials will tarry, assuming the charges to be justified; greater will be the impediments in fostering democracy, which is not a plant of easy growth. If prosecutions which the Bill envisages are allowed to have their normal, leisurely span of anything between 5 to 10 years, no fruitful purpose will be served by launching them. Speedy termination of prosecutions under the Bill is the heart and soul of the Bill".

73. That the power of the judicature could not be 'usurped or infringed' by the executive or the legislature. The Privy Council examined the other objectionable provisions of the amended Act and held that they were these provisions are not relevant for purposes of the present case, but I cannot help extracting the following note of caution struck by their Lordships:

"What is done once, if it be allowed, may be done again and in a lesser crisis and less serious circumstances; and thus judicial power may be eroded."

An attempt like the one made in the present Bill to usurp an important judicial power and vest it in the executive, is a serious inroad on the independence of the judiciary and is fraught with serious consequences. It has therefore necessarily to be put down at the very inception for it may otherwise give rise to a prospect too gruesome to envisage and too dangerous to be allowed to have the sanction of law,"

74. Sufficient guideline was provided in the preamble of the reported case unlike the PSA, Besides that, though there is a provision for making rule under section 25 of the PSA but no such rules have, for reasons known to the Government, been framed till date.

75. The learned Attorney-General also argued that the question is whether the law giving direction to the executive has provided any guideline or stated the policy and it has to be determined by reading the statute including its preamble and that there are instances where laws apparently conferring unguided discretion were held valid by the Indian Supreme Court and cited the case of 131 Irani vs Madras, AIR 1961 SC 1731 and Rayala Corporation vs Director of Exchange Control, AIR 1970 SC 494. Mr Abdur Razzaq submitted that those cases are clearly different and distinguishable from the PSA case. The power was to be exercised to further the policy and the purpose of the Act namely, to prevent unreasonable eviction of tenants.
