76. In the Special Courts Bill 1978, AIR 1979 SC 478 discussed earlier the Supreme Court of India gave its opinion that the Bill with the only exception that the special court would be presided by a retired Judge of the High Court of India is constitutionally valid. That Bill as has been quoted in extensor will show that it had an exceptionally long title/preamble giving a clear guideline as to why it was necessary to create additional Courts. Section 4(1) of the Bill was of particular importance because it gave a clear guideline as to which persons would be tried by the special court which runs as follows:

4(1) ''If the central government is of the 'opinion that there is prima facie evidence of the commission of an offence alleged to have been committed during the period mentioned in the preamble by a person who held high public or political office in India and that in accordance with the guidelines contained in the preamble hereto the said offence ought to be dealt with under the Act, the central Government shall make a declaration to that effect in every case in which it is of the aforesaid opinion."

77. In our own jurisdiction we do have an appropriate case where the law was declared ultra vires and void for lack of guidelines. On a reading of the PSA, it is abundantly clear that it allows the police an arbitrary and unguided discretion to apply the law and on this ground it is unconstitutional and void being discriminatory and violative of the equality provision of the Constitution. Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed and Mr Abdur Razzaque relied on the case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh 33 DLR (AD) 201 in which case their Lordships held "after having considered the arguments of the learned Counsel and the cases cited by him in support of his contentions that section 9(2) of the Public Servants Retirement Act, 1974 providing for compulsory retirement of public servants completing 25 years of service was challenged on the ground that the law, conferring discretion on the government to retire a public servant without providing any guideline, was violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution upon consideration of a large number of decisions including Jibendra Kishore, East and West Steamship Co. Waris Meah, Munim J (with whom Ruhul Islam and BH Chowdhury JJ agreed) observed:

"The minimum principle or guideline as has been provided in service rules as appeared from the cases in this judgment is that of the public servant or the interest of public service. In either the impugned Act or the rules made thereunder provided such principle, the minimum requirement of law as showing the existence of some guideline for the exercise of discretion in retiring a Government servant who has completed 25 years of service would, I think, be satisfied, thus making it immune from any challenge on the ground of discrimination violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. I am of opinion therefore, that in the absence of such a guideline either in the Act or the rules framed thereunder, section 9(2) suffers from unconstitutionality. Dr Nurul Islam and 3 others were retired under section 9(2) as they completed 25 years of service although there were 31 others who had also completed 25 years of service. Dr Nurul Islam was replaced by Dr Maniruzzaman who was senior to Dr Islam both in age and service by three years. This could be done because there was no guideline as to how the selection for compulsory retirement would be made. Previously there was a guideline namely "in the public interest." This was omitted and was not in place when Dr Islam was retired. After Dr Nurul Islam successfully challenged his retirement the guideline of public interest was once again inserted by way of amendment and the decision in Mafizur Rahman's case 34 DLR (AD) 321 was different. On the right to equality Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh said.

"Article 27 provides that all citizens are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of law. It combines the English concept of equality before law and the American concept of equal protection of law." Equality before law' means that among equals law shall be equal and shall be equally administered. There shall not be any special privilege by reason of birth, creed, etc. 'Equal protection of law' means that all persons in like circumstances shall be treated alike and no discrimination shall be made in conferment of privileges or imposition of liabilities. The first part is negative while the second is positive in approach. Equality before law is involved in the enforcement of law, while equal protection of law involves the validity of a law. But these are not independent or severable concepts in their application and will often be found to overlap each other. This article more than others firmly embodies the concept of rule of law, the establishment of which is one of the prime objectives of the Constitution."

"The principle enunciated by the Indian Supreme Court that a law will not be held discriminatory when unguided discretion is given to a high and responsible officer on the expectation that the discretion will he exercised reasonably is difficult to accept. The expression 'reasonable' is vacuous unless used with reference to a specific standard and in the absence of a standard no exercise of discretion can be judged for reasonableness. Furthermore, in our society we have found high and responsible officers acting arbitrarily even though such arbitrariness is hard to prove in the absence of any standard of reasonableness, particularly in the face of presumption of legality of official acts. In Dr Nurul Islam's case the government urged the principle, but the Appellate Division rightly did not accept the principle even though the discretion was conferred on the government itself."

"In the service rules of statutory corporations often a power is given to the corporation to terminate the services of permanent employees without assigning any reason with notice of a fixed period or pay for that period in lieu of notice. This is purely a grant of unfettered and uncanalised power to select employees for termination without any guideline whatsoever and on the principle enunciated in Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh such a grant of power is violative of Article 27 of the Constitution. In several cases, the Indian Supreme Court declared such a power of termination to be violative of the equality clause. The High Court Division set aside an order of termination of service of several employees of Parjatan Corporation under Rule 41(2)(i)(a) of the corporation's service rules which permitted the corporation to terminate the services of employees without assigning any reason by giving notice of a fixed period or paying salary of the notice period. The Appellate Division set aside the order of the High Court Division in Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation vs Shahid Hossain. It could very well be argued that the rule conferring unfettered discretion on the corporation was violative of Article 27, but no such argument was advanced."

"Contemporaneous law and retrospectively: Article 31 guarantees that an individual shall be dealt with in accordance with law. Thus an individual cannot be prejudicially affected unless there is contemporaneously in existence a legal provision to sustain the action. A person shall not be prevented from or hindered in doing an act which is not prohibited by law. A public functionary in discharge of his official function taking away a car of an individual without any authority of law, the action is not only illegal, but also violative of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 31. The question is, whether Parliament can retrospectively validate an act which was unconstitutional because of the absence of any contemporaneous law to sustain the act. The Appellate Division in Mofizur Rahman vs Bangladesh answered the question in the affirmative. The provision of section 9(2) of the Public Servants Retirement Act, 1974 conferring a discretion on the government to retire public servants on completion of 25 years of service was declared void by the Appellate Division as being discriminatory for want of any guideline for the exercise of the discretion. As a result, all actions under the Act retiring public servants became unconstitutional. Section 9(2) was later amended providing the guideline of 'public interest' and the amending Act validated the previous actions retiring public servants. The court referred to a number of decisions of the Indian Supreme Court, the British Indian Federal Court and the Australian High Court and took note of the difference in language between Article 31 and Article 35 to hold that the expression "in accordance with law" does not mean "in accordance with law in force" at the time of taking action and upheld the amending Act validating the unconstitutional actions of retirement of public servants. It is submitted that reference to the decisions of the Indian Supreme Court is inappropriate inasmuch as the Indian Constitution does not contain any provision similar to Article 31. The same was the position under the Government of India Act, 1935 and in the Australian jurisdiction. A noted author criticised the Indian Supreme Court for not considering whether those validating laws were reasonable restrictions within the meaning of Article 19 of the Indian Constitution and made a comparative study of the British, Canadian, Australian and Indian positions. The absence of the expression 'in force at the time of commission of the act' may be important in determining the permissibility of retrospective laws. The difference in language is there because the framers of the Constitution did not intend to take away the power of Parliament to enact retrospective laws which do not offend the constitutional limitation, but from the said difference of language an interpretation cannot be given to permit Parliament to avoid the constitutional limitation of Article 31 or render Article 31 nugatory. In the American jurisdiction, the legislature has the power to pass retrospective laws if the retrospectively does not offend any provision of the constitution including the 'due process' clause. When a law is passed, the retrospective aspect of the legislation, as well as the prospective aspects, must meet the test of due process and the justifications for the latter may not suffice for the former. Even when the court finds the law (operating prospectively) valid under the due process clause, the court will have the further duty to inquire whether the retrospective operation given to the law is unreasonable or arbitrary, or, in other words, the court will inquire whether there was a rational relationship between the retrospectively and the legitimate governmental interest sought to be achieved by the retrospectively. When a retrospective law is once covered by Article 35 no question of reasonableness will arise, and the very fact that the law is retrospective will be sufficient for the court to declare it void. The question of reasonableness will be moot when such law is not covered by Article 35. Parliament has power to make retrospective laws; the only limitation is that like all other laws it must pass the test of constitutionality under Article 31 and the retrospectively must not be arbitrary or unreasonable. If the retrospectively is found to be arbitrary or unreasonable, it will be violative of Article 31 and therefore void."

A law will not pass the test' of Article 31 if it is found to be vague, uncertain or in excess of the requirement as stated in the foregoing paragraph."

109. Mr Mainul Hosein, learned Counsel appearing in Writ Petition No. 192 of 2001 (the 16 lawyers case), termed the PSA as a black and repressive law on the ground, amongst others, that it has usurped the power of the judiciary. He submits that "In a pending case the power and discretion to grant or not to grant bail is a judicial function and not a legislative one. It is a different matter that under the law of preventive detention a person is detained by administrative order in the absence of any criminal proceeding. But when a criminal proceeding has started and the accused is produced before the Magistrate by police in compliance with Article 33(2) of the Constitution within 24 hours, the judicial power and protection available to the arrested person is the exercise of judicial power. Article 33(2) is for providing judicial protection and judicial custody to an accused facing trial. But that has been negated by section 16 of the Public Safety Act.

110. Article 116A of the Constitution provides "all persons employed in the judicial service and all Magistrates shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial function." It is this principle of independence of the judiciary which must be kept in mind while interpreting the relevant provision of the Constitution and it was so held in Anwar Hossain vs Bangladesh, relying on AIR 1982 SC 152 SP Gupta and others vs Present of India.

111. Mr Nazmul Huda argues that the PSA, particularly section 16, is ultra vires Article 33(2) of the Constitution. Furthermore, it offends Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution as well.

112. Mr Shafique Ahmed learned Counsel adopted the arguments advanced by Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed and Dr Kamal Hossain. He submits that there is total absence of guidelines in the PSA affording a petty Police Officer like an ASI on his whim and caprice to hook up similarly situated persons (having committed identical offence) under the Penal Code and the PSA as he chooses to do.

113. Mr Ruhul Kuddus learned Counsel appearing in Writ Petition No. 1274 of 2001 took us through two different first information reports lodged on identical allegations one under sections 143/147/341/354/323/427/ 380/ 114 of the Penal Code and the other one under sections 7(Ka)/8/12 of the PSA. He submits that this could happen because of the absence of guidelines provided either in the preamble or under section 3 of the PSA or in the rules which were never framed under section 25 of the PSA as argued by the learned Attorney-General. Mr Ruhul Kuddus argued that very wide powers have been conferred upon the police and they have been using the same most arbitrarily and whimsically. He then submits that this is contrary to rule of law and that arbitrariness and rule of law are sworn enemies and cannot coexist. He referred to Mr Mahmudul Islam's Constitutional Law of Bangladesh on Rule of Law (1.82) at page 52 which is as follows:

"The preamble of the Constitution of Bangladesh states 'rule of law' as one of the objectives to be attained. The expression "rule of law" has various shades of meaning and it is an ever expanding concept. AV Dicey's concept of rule of law included three things—(i) absence of arbitrary power, that is, no man is above law and the persons in authority do not enjoy wide, arbitrary or discretionary powers, (ii) equality before law, and jurisdiction of ordinary courts, and (iii) individual liberties. His thesis has been criticised from many angles, but his emphasis on subjection of every person to the ordinary laws of the land, the absence of arbitrary power and legal protection for certain basic human rights remains the undisputed theme of the doctrine of rule of law. According to Professor Wade rule of law connotes three ideas—(1) it expresses a preference for law and order within a community rather than anarchy, warfare and constant strife, (2) it expresses a legal doctrine of fundamental importance, namely, that government must be conducted according to law, and that in disputed cases what the law requires is declared by judicial decisions and (3) it refers to a body of political opinion about what the declared rules on law should provide in matters both of substance and of procedure. The first two ideas are not sufficient in achieving a democratic society in which human dignity and freedom may be ensured, for, in a dictatorship, law and order can be maintained and the government can be run in accordance with law promulgated by the dictator and yet there may not be any freedom of the people if the law make by the dictator does not provide for such freedom. For this the third idea is added to make the concept a meaningful one. "Law in the context of the rule of law does not mean any law enacted by the legislative authorities, however arbitrary or despotic it may be what is necessary element of the rule of law it that law must not be arbitrary or irrational and it must satisfy the test of reason and the democratic form of the polity seeks to ensure this element by making the framer of the law accountable to the people," The concept is now intended to imply not only that (1) the powers exercised by State functionaries must have a legal basis, that is, they must be based on authority conferred by law, but also that (ii) the law should conform to certain minimum standards of justice, both substantive and procedural." The concept implies that the ruler must also be subject to law. It is the subordination of all authorities, legislative, executive and others to certain principles which would generally be accepted as characteristic of law, such as the ideas of the fundamental principles of justice, normal principles, fairness and due process. It implies respect for the supreme value and dignity of the individual. "It is generally agreed that the minimum content of the concept is that "the law affecting individual liberty ought to be reasonably certain or predictable; where the law confers wide discretionary powers there should be adequate safeguards against their abuse; like should be treated alike, and unfair discrimination must not be sanctioned by law; a person ought not to be deprived of his liberty, status or any other substantial interest unless he is given the opportunity of a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal; and so forth. "The rule of law demands that power is to be exercised in a manner which is just, fair and reasonable and not in an unreasonable, capricious or arbitrary manner leaving room for discrimination. It requires that decisions should be made by the application of known principles and rules and in general, such decisions should be predictable and the citizen should know where he stands; a decision without any principle or rule is unpredictable and is the antithesis of a decision in accordance with the rule of law.

114. In the case of I. Manila vs Dr H Borobabur AIR 1994 SC 505 when a Speaker of a state legislature refused to appear before the Indian Supreme Court to answer the charge of contempt of court committed by him by acts not performed as Speaker within the House, the court directed the government to produce him before the court, observing:

"It is our constitutional duty which requires us to make this order, to uphold the majesty of law and justify the confidence of the people, that no one in this country is above the law and governance is not of men but of the 'rule of law'. It is unfortunate that this action has to be taken against a person who happens to be the Speaker of a Legislative Assembly, but that does not permit us to apply the law differently to him when he has willfully and contumaciously driven the Court to this course. We must remind ourselves that the 'rule of law' permits no one to claim to be above the law and it means 'be you ever so high the law is above you.'

The International Commission of Justice endeavoured to give material content to the concept in a Congress in New Delhi in 1959 which was attended by eminent jurists from more than fifty countries including Lord Denning and Lord Devlin. That Congress made a declaration known as the Declaration of Delhi, 1959. The "rule of law" according to that declaration relates to:

(1) the Legislature: there is a right to representative and responsible government; and there are certain minimum standards or principles for the law, including those contained in the Universal Declaration and the European Convention, in particular, freedom of religious belief, assembly and association, and the absence of retroactive penal laws:

(2) the Executive, especially that delegated legislation, should be subject to independent judicial control, and that a citizen who is wronged should have a remedy against the State or Government;

(3) the Criminal Process; a "fair trial" involves such elements as certainty of the criminal law, the presumption of innocence, reasonable rules relating to arrest, accusation and detention pending trial, the giving of notice, and provision for legal advice, public trial, right of appeal and absence of cruel or unusual punishment;

(4) the Judiciary and the Legal Profession; this requires the independence of the Judiciary, and proper grounds and procedure for removal of judges; and imposes a responsibility upon an organised and autonomous legal profession.

115. The rule of law is a basic feature of the Constitution of Bangladesh. To attain this fundamental aim of the State, the Constitution has made substantive provisions for the establishment of a polity where ever functionary of the State must justify his action with reference to law. 'Law' does not mean anything that Parliament may pass. Articles 27 and 31 have taken care of the qualitative aspects of law. Article 27 forbids discrimination in law or in State actions, while Article 31 imports the concept of due process, both substantive and procedural, and thus prohibits arbitrary or unreasonable law or State action. The Constitution further guarantees in Part III certain rights to ensure respect for the supreme value of human dignity

116. Mr Justice MH Rahman in the case of Anwar Hossain vs Bangladesh, BLD Special Issue 1989 (the 8th Amendment case) held "I am however, striking down amendment not on the ground of uncertainties or irreconcilability of the existing provisions with the amended provisions, as such, but on the ground of the amendment's irreconcilability with the rule of law, as envisaged in the preamble, and in furtherance of which Articles 27, 31, 32, 44, 94 to 116A were particularly incorporated in the Constitution.

117. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Attorney-General, argued that under Article 82 no Money Bill or any bill involving expenditure of the Government shall be presented to Parliament unless recommended by the President, Purpose being that such a Bill should not be presented by any private Members Bill and that as the President has to act in this matter on the advice of the Prime Minister, the former has no option but to recommend such Bill when placed before him. The bill in question (PSA) was signed by the Prime Minister and whether the Bill was actually Money Bill or a Bill involving expenditure of the government money would have to be signed by the President. In that view it is of no consequence that the Bill was presented before the President as a Bill involving expenditure of the government. This argument in my view suffers from two fallacies:

(1) True it is that the President was duty bound to sign those Bills for their introduction into the Parliament in their true colour and character either as Money Bill or as a Bill involving expenditure of the Government. But the extract Bill Annexure "C" to Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000 at para 5 clearly pointed out the Bill (PSA) as a Bill involving expenditure of Public Moneys for President's recommendation. It was not sent as a Money Bill and the President did recommend it as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not as a Money Bill.

(2) Secondly, why the Bill was not marked as a Money Bill for the President's recommendation? The reason is obvious. It was not a Money Bill under Article 81(1) of the Constitution. In paragraph 7 of his affidavit-in-opposition the learned Attorney-General tried to justify that the PSA was a Money Bill because it was placed before the Parliament as a Money Bill within the meaning of Article 81(1)(d) of the Constitution; that it was accordingly processed with prior recommendation of the President as required under Article 82 and that the Speaker "endorsed a certificate to it as a "Money Bill" as required under Article 81(3) of the Constitution. It is seen that Article 81(1)(d) speaks of imposition of a charge upon the consolidated fund or the alteration or abolition of any such charge which Article 88 without any ambiguity enumerates the expenditure that may be charged upon the consolidated fund which for the purpose of refreshing our memory may once again be reproduced therein below :

(a) the remuneration payable to the President and other expenditure relating to his office;

(b) the remuneration payable to—

(i) the Speaker and Deputy Speaker;

(ii) the Judges of the [Supreme Court];

(iii) the Comptroller and Auditor-General;

(iv) the Election Commissioners;

(v) the members of the Public Service Commissions;

(c) the administrative expresses of, including remuneration payable to, officers and servants of Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the Election Commission and the Public Service Commission;

(d) all debt charges for which the Government is liable, including interest, sinking fund charges, the repayment or amortisation of capital, and other expenditure in connection with the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt;

(e) any sums required to satisfy a judgment, decree or an award against the Republic by any court or tribunal; and

(f) any other expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund by this Constitution or by Act of Parliament.

<u>118. So, the argument that the Bill was a Money Bill must fail. Besides that, the President did never recommend the Bill as a Money Bill as it was not sent for his recommendation as a Money Bill and the endorsement of the Speaker of the Bill as a Money Bill under Article 81(3) being without authority and power is a nullity and the certificate not being a magic wand had no mesmerism to transform a non Money Bill into a Money Bill in derogation of Article 81(1) of the Constitution. The Speaker derives his power of certificate under Article 81(3) which is hedged with a condition that "Every Money Bill before it is presented to the President for his assent shall bear a certificate under his hand "that". (the underlining is mine) it is a Money Bill" and such certificate shall be conclusive for all purposes and shall not be questioned in any court. The expression "that" it is a Money Bill is not an "idle expression or mere formality". It means that the Speaker must satisfy himself that what he is presenting for the assent of the President is, in fact, a Money Bill. And that satisfaction must be derived from the enumeration given under Article 81(1)(a) to (f) read with Articles 81(2) and 88 of the Constitution. Furthermore, Article 7(1) which is the "touch stone" of the Constitution ordains in no uncertain term that "All powers in the Republic belong to the people and their exercise on behalf of the people shall be effected only under, and by authority of this Constitution while under Article 7(2) it is sanctified to be the "solemn expression" of the will of the people and the "Supreme law of the Republic". Now the question is, have the people invested the Speaker with the power or, in other words, is the Speaker empowered to certify a Bill as a Money Bill which, in fact, is not a Money Bill? The answer must be "no". The power conferred upon the Speaker under Article 81(3) must be exercised on behalf of the people and must be affected only under, and by authority, of the Constitution. This sacred document (the Constitution) has not authorised or invested anyone, specially the constitutional functionaries of the state who are under oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution to issue a false certificate transgressing the presidential prerogative under Article 80(3) of the Constitution. This constitutional power cannot be negated and denied by anyone at his sweet will or whim. There must be a clear and unambiguous conferment of such power by the Constitution itself. In the facts and circumstances of this case, particularly the way the extract Bill was sent to the President for his recommendation to be introduced in the House, the way the Home Minister deliberately misled the House saying that the President recommended the Bill as a Money Bill (which it was not) and the way the Speaker sent the Bill for the assent of the President after it was passed by the Parliament as a Money Bill certifying that the Bill (PSA) was a Money Bill knowing fully well that it was not so under Article 81(1) of the Constitution, I am left with but only one conclusion that it was a ploy to pre-empt the prerogative of the President (under Article 80(3) to prevent him from refusing or withholding his assent to the Bill and returning it back to the Parliament because it did not answer the description of a Money Bill enumerated under clauses (a) to (f) of sub-Article (1) of Article 81 of the Constitution. It was clearly an act of fraud by the Speaker committed upon the President, upon the Constitution and, above all, upon the people.</u>

119. The Supreme Court derives its powers under Articles 101, 102, 109, 110 of the Constitution. All authorities, executive and judicial, in the Republic shall act in aid of the Supreme Court" (Article 112). If however, the Bill (PSA) in terms of Article 81(1) was a Money Bill, the certificate given by the Speaker that it was a Money Bill would, of course, be conclusive for all purposes and, as such, immune from judicial review. But since the Bill was not a Money Bill and the certificate of the Speaker was used as a mechanism to practice fraud upon the Constitution and it denuded the President of his prerogative under Article 80(3) of the Constitution it cannot be allowed to claim any immunity from judicial review of the Constitutional Court.

120. The Parliament under Article 65(1) is vested with the legislative power of the Republic subject to the provision of the Constitution. That being so, can the Parliament enact a Law (here the PSA) denying bail as has been done under section 16 of the PSA which right existed under section 497(1) and (2) of the CrPC long before the Constitution came into being in the face of the Constitutional Provision laid down under Article 101 saying: The High Court Division shall have such original, appellate and other jurisdictions, powers and functions as are (the underlining is mine) or may be conferred on it by this Constitution or any other law? Can the Parliament pass a law calling for a sentence of imprisonment for life allowing the Tribunal who is a Sessions Judge to record only the substance of the testimony of a witness to the detriment of the accused in his appeal against conviction because in a criminal appeal the whole case i.e facts and law, are laid bare before the appellate Court and the sifting, appreciation and evaluation of evidence may differ from judge to judge and in the absence of the entire evidence the appellant is bound to be gravely prejudiced in his defence thus causing serious miscarriage of justice? Can the Parliament pass a law allowing the statement of a witness recorded under section 164 CrPC to be used as evidence to corroborate other evidence without being examined as a witness at the trial as has been provided for under section 14(3) of the PSA? Can the Parliament pass a law taking away the inherent power of the court under section 561A of the CrPC or for that matter the power under sections 439 and 526 of the CrPC as has been done under section 24 of the PSA? The answer I am afraid is a resounding and emphatic "no". And if the Parliament knew that in the guise of a Money Bill they are passing a law denying citizens of their fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution and the existing laws, they would have shuddered to disown and throw it into the dungeon.

121. In Paragraph 44 of his written submission it has been stated and strenuously argued by the learned Attorney-General that by the mere mentioning of a section of the PSA by a Police Officer in the first information report a citizen's liberty cannot be curtailed because the Magistrate has the right and duty to see from the allegation made whether a case under the impugned Act (PSA) has been made out or not. The allegation he asserts is mere accusation and if it does not substantially disclose the commission of an offence under the impugned Act, the accusation will not come under the purview of the impugned Act, and hence the Magistrate can grant ball. Article 33(2) requires the production of the arrested person before the Magistrate and if the Magistrate does not apply his judicial mind to determine whether there is substantial information as to commission of offence under the PSA it is the failure of the Magistrate in performing his duty for which remedy lies to the higher court, but the law cannot be held to be void because the abuse of the law cannot render the law void: every law carries the possibility of abuse by the persons entrusted with the enforcement of law." In Paragraph 45 of the written submission he maintained and argued "that in the United States bail is an absolute right except in capital cases but in our country in all cases of serious nature, it is non-bail able and bar to grant bail is nothing new. Section 497 of the CrPC prohibits grant of bail in offences punishable not only with death but also with imprisonment for life. (It may be noted that in consideration of the social condition Pakistan amended section 497 of the CrPC prohibiting grant of bail also in case of offences punishable with 10 years imprisonment).  The underlining is that of the learned Attorney-General. He further argues that it is true that a man will suffer if any untrue allegation is made, that a man suffers when a false allegation of murder or even worse when he is accused of offences under section 436 (arson) or 459 (grievous hurt inflicted in the course of lurking house trespass) but it cannot render section 497 CrPC void. Under section 497 CrPC, the Magistrate must deny bail when there is reasonable ground for believing that the accused has committed an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. In PSA the Magistrate has to refuse bail when there is substantial information about commission of an offence under the Act. It may be remembered, argued the learned Attorney-General, that substantial information at the initial stage offers a reasonable ground for believing that a man is guilty of an offence. In this regard the following statement of the American position on Bail made by Schwartz in his Constitutional Law 1st Ed. page 198 may be considered.

122. The essential line is that between mere suspicion and probable case. For the case to fall on the probable cause side there must be evidence that reasonably supports the belief that the required legal justification for the arrest exists. The evidence may be circumstantial in nature or may even consist of factual information given by the informer" (emphasis added by the Attorney-General). I am afraid this argument of the learned Attorney-General on bail is fallacious and, as such, cannot be accepted firstly, because the language used in section 16 of the PSA is miles apart in their import from that of the authority referred to. Under section 16 of the PSA no accused can be granted bail whatever may be the offence before 90 days by the Tribunal, Appellate Court (High Court) or any other court. Besides that, the American and Pakistani positions on bail are of no consequence in the face of section 497 of the Bangladesh CrPC because under the said section there is a bar to the granting of bail only where the alleged offence is non-bail able and there is reason to believe that the accused is guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life but even in those cases the court can grant bail if the accused is a person below 16 years of age or a woman, or sick or infirm and under sub-section (2) of section 497 CrPC the accused is entitled to bail as of right if at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial there is sufficient ground for further inquiry. So, section 16 of the PSA., the amendment made in Pakistan of section 497 CrPC and the American position cannot be equated with section 497 of our CrPC, Apart from that, in the face of the total embargo placed under section 16 of the PSA how can the Magistrate grant bail before submission of police report? And rightly the Magistrate refused to entertain application for bail in Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000 arising out of GR Case No. 381 of 2000 by his order dated 9-8-2000 saying “অত্র মামলার জামিন শুনানীর এখতিয়ার অত্র আদালতের নাই। এমতাবস্থায় আবেদন নথিভূক্ত করা হল।” Had he not done so he would also be placed under suspension like SI Matin who recorded Khulsi Khulna PS Case No. 15 dated 26-12-2000 giving rise to Writ Petition No. 76 of 2000 against Mr Morshed Khan MP and his son.

123. Section 497 CrPC unlike section 16 of the PSA does not deny the jurisdiction and power of courts and does not run contrary to the fundamental right of the petitioners guaranteed under Article 33(2) of the Constitution. Section 16 of the PSA is therefore, without any doubt ultra vires to Article 33(2) of the Constitution and, as such, void. It is also void for contravening Article 116A of the Constitution which enjoins that "subject to the Provisions of the Constitution, all persons employed in the judicial service and all magistrates shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial functions inasmuch as under section 16 of the PSA the Magistrate has been transferred into a lame, deaf and dumb duck. We have been hearing for a pretty long time (for over 40 years) that there should be separation of power of the judiciary from the executive. All the political parties while they are not in power speak with passionate eloquence about the necessity of separation of power but once they change position and form the government very quickly and conveniently they forget their promise, and pledge. They always keep the magistracy under their executive control instead of placing them and making them answerable and accountable to the Sessions Judge and ultimately, the Supreme Court. Had the Magistrates been under the judicial control of the Sessions Judge and that of the Supreme Court, there could be no violation of Article 116A of the Constitution and there could be no law like section 16 of the PSA. The Magistrates can never act independently so long they are under the control of the Executive in spite of Article 116A and 33(2) of the Constitution. It should be the sacred duty of the legislature to pass a law placing the Magistrates under the control of the Supreme Court to secure fair and impartial justice from them in discharge of their judicial functions. It is a shame for a Magistrate to say “অত্র মামলার জামিন শুনানীর এখতিয়ার অত্র আদালতের নাই।”

124. The argument of the learned Attorney-General that recording of the substance of the evidence instead of the testimony in its entirety as provided under section 18(1)(Kha) of the PSA does not in any way prejudice the accused in his defence because if the tribunal does not record the material evidence, it is a failure of duty of the tribunal for which the law cannot be bad and that if the tribunal omits something which is material, the accused can by filing a petition bring it to the notice of the tribunal and if the tribunal does not act on it, the matter can be agitated in the appellate Court, (the High Court Division) cannot but be said to be an ingenious and novel procedure because the accused is not required by law to prove anything in support of his innocence except when he sets up a plea of alibi. The burden of proof in a criminal case lies wholly and solely on the prosecution and it never shifts as it happens in civil cases. Because of the presumption of innocence the accused has nothing to say except that he pleads not guilty and claims to be tried. The prosecution must prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt. Inquisitorial system of criminal jurisprudence is an alien concept in the Anglo Saxon system which we have adopted. Thus section 18(1)(Kha) of the PSA is ultra vires the Constitution and void. The learned Attorney-General also defended section 14(3) of the PSA as to the use of a statement of a witness recorded under section 164 CrPC as evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act. This is also a novel concept alien to the law of evidence because such a statement can only be used by the defence to contradict the prosecution witness whereas under section 14(3) of the PSA the benefit is sought to be given to the prosecution instead of to the accused. This is against the rule of law as well as the due process of law and thus void.

125. I do not disagree with the learned Attorney-General that under Rule 33 of the Rules of Business the Prime Minister may in a particular case permit or condone departure or deviation from the prescribed rules as to initiation of a Bill and that being so the respondent claiming the PSA (before it was passed and assented to) as a Money Bill having been initiated by the Ministry of Home Affairs instead of by the Ministry of Finance which is the usual and proper procedure cannot be taken exception to because it was signed by the Prime Minister. But the moot question is otherwise. It is clear from Annexure "C" to Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000 that the extract of the PSA that was sent to the President was unmistakably marked at Paragraph 5 not as a Money Bill rather as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys (of course the Bill was signed by the Hon'ble Prime Minister as well as the Home Minister) for the recommendation of the President to be introduced into the house of Parliament and the President did recommend it not as a Money Bill but as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys which is apparent on the face of annexure "C". Furthermore, the President by issuing a public statement which is most unusual, categorically denied to have recommended the Bill as a Money Bill maintaining that what was sent to him was an extract of a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not a Money Bill (Annexure G-(1) “জন নিরাপত্তা বিলটি অর্থ বিল হিসেবে দেখানো হয়নি।” Annexure-H(1) was also to the same effect (জননিরাপত্তা আইনটি আমার কাছে অর্থ বিল হিসেবে দেখানো হয়নি). But strangely enough it is found from Annexure "5" of the affidavit-in-opposition by respondent No. 1 (Government of Bangladesh) that Mr Mohammad Nasim the Home Minister introduced the PSA into the Parliament as a Money Bill telling the Legislature that the Hon'ble President had recommended the Bill as a Money Bill for its introduction into the Parliament. The Home Minister misled the Parliament and induced them to pass it as a Money Bill though it was not a Money Bill in terms of Article 81(1) of the Constitution. Nobody is disputing the competency of the Parliament to enact laws but it must be, subject to the provision of the Constitution (Article 65). So unlike the Parliament at Westminster it has a limited power. It does not have they Plenary Power of the British Parliament in enacting laws. Now the question arises as to whether the Parliament has the power to pass the PSA as a Money Bill? The answer must be in the negative. The PSA is a colorable legislation and thus a fraud on the Constitution inasmuch as the Parliament had no competence to pass such a Bill as a Money Bill. Parliament has indirectly sought to enact a law in the guise of a Money Bill which could never have been enacted under Article 81(1) of the Constitution as a Money Bill. Such legislation is a colorable legislation and is void as has been explained and accepted by the Appellate Division in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319.

126. The learned Attorney-General submits that the constitutional validity of the law (PSA) cannot be questioned as under Article 78(1) of the Constitution there is an embargo and in support cited the case of Bradlaugh vs Gossett (1884) 12 QBD 271, British Railways Board vs Pickin (1974) AC 765 = (1974) 1 AER 609 and Ahmed Saeed Kirmani PLD 1958 SC 397. Those cases are different and distinguishable. Those were concerned with the internal transactions of the Parliament and those did not transgress their limits but in the case of PSA the Parliament overstepped and transgressed its limits prescribed under Article 1(1) of the Constitution in passing a non-Money Bill as a Money Bill and hence Article 78(1) cannot prevent the court from exercising its power of judicial review of unconstitutional acts.

127. Article 78(1) cannot protect the PSA firstly, because it is a colorable legislation and the Parliament had no competence to pass the same as a Money Bill in terms of Article 81(1) of the Constitution and secondly, because it is void for contravening fundamental right guaranteed by Articles 27, 31, 32 and 33 of the Constitution. The English precedents of immunity of Parliamentary Proceedings are on principle unquestionable, but it must be kept in mind that in England the courts do not have the power or jurisdiction to review legislative act. The Courts in England interpret and apply the law. All the cases cited by the learned Attorney-General are unnecessary and need not be gone into because with regard to the proceedings of Parliament the position in our jurisdiction, amongst others, is that if the Parliament oversteps or transgresses its limits under the Constitution, Article 78(1) will not prevent the courts from exercising their power of judicial review of unconstitutional acts. In the Special Courts Bill, 1978 AIR 1979 SC 478 Chandrachud CJ (for himself and on behalf of PN Bhagwati, PS Sarkaria and S Murtaza Fazal Ali, JJ held : "the British Parliament being supreme, no question can arise in England as regards the validity of laws passed by it. The position under our Constitution is fundamentally different because, the validity of laws passed by the Indian legislatures has to be tested having regard to the scheme of distribution of legislative powers and on the anvil of other constitutional limitations like those contained in Article 13 of our Constitution (Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights). The right of the Indian judiciary to pronounce a legislation void if it conflicts with the Constitution is not merely a tacit assumption but is an express avowal of our Constitution. The principle is so firmly and wisely embedded in our Constitution that the policy of law and the expediency of passing it are matters for the legislature to decide while interpretation of law and questions regarding their validity fall within the exclusive advisory or adjudicatory functions of the courts. The functions of courts in that behalf is not "The great usurpation" as some American critics of the power of judicial review called it after the American Supreme Court rendered its decision in Dred-Scott in (1856)15 LEd. 691.

128. The learned Attorney-General then used his tramp card of the blanket coverage provided under Article 81(3) of the Constitution ousting the jurisdiction of Court. In this respect I do not have the slightest of doubts that this blanket is neither heavy nor large enough to shield the NA from the judicial review of the constitutional Court. The Speaker gives the certificate because of the power granted to him under Article 81(3) of the Constitution but if it transgresses any provision of the Constitution it is not immune from judicial review. The certificate- clearly and unmistakably transgressed Article 81(1). Secondly, it denied the President's right to exercise the power of returning the Bill back to the Parliament as provided under Article 80(3) i.e. Bills other than a Money Bill by fraudulently certifying the Bill as a Money Bill. A Law resulting from such transgression is also void under Article 7(1) and 7(2) of the Constitution. The Speaker has not been given the power to certify a non Money Bill as a Money Bill nor has he been given the power to tread on the toes of the President, push him aside and denude him of his constitutional prerogative given under Article 80(3) of the Constitution. In that view of the matter the decisions relied on by the learned Attorney-General in the case of RV Registrar Companies, ex parte Central Bank of India (1986) 1 QBD 114 and the case of Anisminic Ltd. vs Foreign Compensation Tribunal (1969) 2 AC 147 are of no help to the respondents.

129. On Section 18(1)(Kha) of the PSA which provides for substance of the evidence to be recorded instead of the testimony in its boiled form and section 18(1)(Ka) of the said Act provides that the procedure under Chapter XX of the CrPC insofar as it is applicable shall be followed. Offences calling for imprisonment for life and triable by the Tribunal who is a Sessions Judge would be allowed to record substance of the evidence and that the Tribunal shall follow the procedure laid down under Chapter XX of the CrPC (of the trial of cases by Magistrate) is by any standard a novel, ingenious and revolutionary idea unknown in the criminal jurisprudence of any civilised country run under a democratic system of government. It is repugnant to the idea of justice. There cannot be a fair trial under the proposed procedure. The accused would be gravely prejudiced and there is bound to be a serious miscarriage of justice which offends and infringes the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 32, 33 and 35 of the Constitution.

The learned Attorney-General in his written ' submission as well as in his argument maintained that:

(1) In determining the constitutionality of a statute, the court is not concerned with the wisdom or justice of the law; the legislature is the judge of it.

(2) A law cannot be unconstitutional on the ground that it violates one or more of the principles of liberty, or the spirit of the Constitution unless such principles or spirit are found in terms of the Constitution and referred to the Constitution of India by HM Seervai Fourth Edition page 262.

(3) It must be presumed that the Legislature understands and correctly appreciates the need of its own people, that its laws are directed to problems made manifest by experience RK Dahnia vs Justice Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 548.

(4) In judging the validity of a law the court shall take notice of matters of common knowledge, matters of common report and the history of the time and shall presume existence of all possible facts which render the law valid.

(5) That the contention of the Counsel for the petitioners that Parliament is not capable of legislating a law terming it as a Money Bill when it is not covered by the definition of Money Bill is not tenable (Paragraph 16 of the written submission). These arguments cannot be accepted because Article 7 speaks of the supremacy not of the Parliament, rather of the Constitution and enjoins that every functionary must perform his duty and exercise his power by and under the authority of the Constitution. Furthermore, the power of the Parliament to legislate is subject to the provision of the Constitution (Article 65(1) of the Constitution). The contentions of the learned Attorney-General have thus no legs to stand on. So I reject this argument of the learned Attorney-General.

(6) The next contention of the learned Attorney-General that though all provisions of the Constitution are of equal importance and all of them are to be given effect to, in case of conflict special provision will prevail over general provision and later provision will prevail over earlier provision. This is tantamount to accepting the rule of the marine and forest world that large animals have the right privilege of gobbling up the smaller and weaker ones. In other words, this sounds like the ‘Orwellian dictum' that 'all animals are equal but some are more equal than others.' It may hold good in a dehumanized authoritarian society but cannot have any acceptability when attempt is made to render one constitutional provision subordinate and subservient to any other Article in its sanctity, degree and dignity. I am nonplussed even to toy with the idea that Articles 7, 26, 27, 31, 32, 33, 35 and 65(1) being earlier provisions can be negated and or downgraded by Articles 78(1) and 81(3) of the Constitution. The legislature can never be presumed to have had such intention. In our Constitution as has been discussed earlier that the Preamble has been entrenched not only in Article 7 but also in the fundamental rights Chapter. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of the Preamble speak of rule of law, fundamental human rights, equality before law and the Supremacy of the Constitution. It is worth mentioning here that the Preamble cannot be amended even under Article 142. It can only be amended by a referendum. So this argument of the learned Attorney-General fails.

130. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Mr Abdur Razzaq and the learned Additional Attorney-General have brought on record a large number of paper cuttings from some of the esteemed and very widely circulated newspapers and in unison with the learned Attorney-General urged upon this Court to take judicial notice of the everyday happenings in the country.

131. Judges are not islands. They like all other individuals are human beings. They are neither robots nor do they live like monks or run in a cloistered monastery, nor do they live in an ivory tower detached from the society shutting their eyes and closing their ears and hence cannot afford to say that "we see no evil and hear no evil. If any Judge tends to do so or, in fact, is seen to be doing so, in my opinion, that would be pernicious, immoral, unethical and, most of" all, conduct unbecoming of a Judge, specially if he happens to be a Judge of a constitutional court. A Judge can never allow the Constitution to be trampled by anyone however high he or she may happen to be. The Constitution is the property of the people. The three organs of the State i.e. the Executive, legislature and the judiciary are the creatures of the Constitution. They are the creatures and the Constitution is the creator. So, they cannot be above the Constitution. It is the Supreme Law of the Republic (Article 7 of the Constitution). For the purpose of refreshing our memory I would. like to take the liberty of repeating what Hamoodur Rahman CJ, said in State vs Ziaur Rahman PLD 1973 SC 49.

"So far, as this court is concerned it has never claimed to be above the Constitution nor to have the right to strike down any provision of the Constitution. It has accepted the position that it is a creature of the Constitution; that it derives its powers and jurisdictions from the Constitution; and that it will event confine itself within the limits set by the Constitution which it has taken oath to protect and preserve but it does claim and has always claimed that it has the right to interpret the Constitution and to say as to what a particular provision of the Constitution means or does not mean, even if that particular provision is a provision seeking to oust the jurisdiction of the Court.

This is a right which it acquires not dehors the Constitution but by virtue of the fact that it is a superior Court set up by the Constitution itself. It is not necessary for this purpose to invoke any divine or supernatural right but this judicial power is inherent in the Court itself. It flows from the fact that it is a Constitutional Court and it can only be taken away by abolishing the Court itself. In saying this, however, I should make it clear that I am making a distinction between 'judicial power' and 'jurisdiction.' In a system where there is a tracheotomy of sovereign powers, then ex necessitate rei from the very nature of things the judicial power must be vested in the judiciary. But what is that judicial power. 'Judicial Power' has been defined in the Corpus Juris Secundum, Vol. XVI, Paragraph 144, as follows:

"The judiciary or judicial department is an intendment and equal coordinate branch of Government, and is that branch thereof which is intended to interpret, construe, and apply the law or that department of Government which is charged with the declaration of what the law is, and its construction, so far as it is written law.'

"This power, it is said, is inherent in the judiciary by reason of the system of division of powers itself under which, as Chief Justice. Marshal put it, 'the Legislature makes, the executive execute, and the judiciary construe, the law'. Thus, the determination of what the existing law is in relation to something already done or happened is the function of the judiciary while the predetermination of what the law shall be for the regulation of all future cases falling under its provisions is the function of the Legislature.

"It may well be asked at this stage as to what is meant by 'jurisdiction'? How does it differ from judicial power'? Apart from setting up the organs, the Constitution may well provide for a great many other things, such as, the subjects in respect of which that power may be exercised and the manner of the exercise of the power. Thus it may provide that the Courts set up will exercise revisional or appellate powers or only decide Constitutional issues. It may demarcate the territories in which a particular Court shall function and over which its writs shall run. It may specify the persons in respect of whom the judicial power to hear and determine will be exercisable. These are all matters which are commonly comprised in what is called the jurisdiction of the Court.

It expresses the concept of the particular res or subject matter over which the judicial power is to be exercised and the manner of its exercise. Jurisdiction is, therefore, a right to adjudicate concerning a particular subject matter in a given case as also the authority to exercise in a particular manner the judicial power vested in the court. "In exercising this power, the judiciary claims no supremacy over other organs of the Government but acts only as the administrator of the public will. Even when it declares a legislative measure unconstitutional and void, it does not do so, because the judicial power is superior in degree or dignity to the legislative power; but because the Constitution has vested it with the power to declare what the law is in the cases which come before it. It thus merely enforces the Constitution as a paramount law whenever a legislative enactment comes into conflict with it because; it is its duty to see that the Constitution prevails. It is only when the Legislature fails to keep within its own Constitutional limits; the judiciary steps in to enforce compliance with the Constitution. This is no doubt a delicate task as pointed out in the case of AK Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs Shah Nawaz, which has to be performed with great circumspection but it has nevertheless to be performed as a sacred constitutional duty when other State functionaries disregard the limitations imposed upon them or claim to exercise power which the people have been careful to withhold from them.

133. He went on saying "Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Court are bound by their oath and duties to act so as to keep the provision of the Constitution fully alive and operative, to preserve it in all respects, save from all defeats or harm and to stand firm in defence of its provisions against attack of any kind.

134. The learned Attorney-General lastly, made a very desperate argument that if the PSA is struck down, the country will plunge into chaos, confusion and utter lawlessness. In his opinion, to curtail and to put an end to abnormal situation by arresting or halting the forward march of the ever increasing rate of crimes harsh law like the PSA is the only solution because it provides for severe and deterrent punishment. I could not persuade myself to agree with or to subscribe to the views of the learned Attorney-General. I am rather of the opinion that it is not the enacting of laws, rather the sincere, faithful and honest enforcement of the law which is required to check lawlessness and crimes. Penal laws in the guise of special enactments made in Bangladesh in the last 30 years will surely exceed Penal laws made in say England for over 200 years. Question may be raised that England is a highly advanced and civilised country so Bangladesh should not be equated with England. It is quite true and logical but can harsh law provide the panacea? Besides the PSA we have some other harsh laws. What result did those laws yield? Take the case of the impugned PSA. After it was enacted has the rate of crime gone down? No. it rather went up. But why?

135. The law enforcing agency is an institution. Its employees are public servants. They must owe allegiance to the State and serve the people. But do they do so? They are not allowed to do so? They have been over the years made to owe allegiance to and serve a class of people having political clout. They serve individuals and parties in power instead of their real masters namely, the people. Through selfish, illegal and partisan use, the Police Department has been allowed to rot and degenerate so much so that it has lost its human face. It has been consistently, unethically and so unscrupulously used as a tool of oppression of the opponents that it has lost its identity beyond recognition. The discipline and the chain of command have totally and completely collapsed. The Police no longer acts as the enforcers of law. In collusion and connivance with the Police, the 'Mastans', under the protective umbrellas of their godfathers sitting in high positions, go on committing crimes against the properties lives and liberties of innocent people with impunity. In presence of police people are maimed and killed and they just play the role of idle spectators. Criminals on many occasions have been reported in the press to have taken shelter in the Police Station on being chased by public. Frequently Police refuse to record first information report against chosen and protected criminals on the plea that “উপরের নির্দেশ রয়েছে কেস না নেওয়ার জন্য” and very often release wanted criminals on the plea of instruction from the top. Rubel, a brilliant and innocent student, was tortured to death at the Police control cell. Yasmin, a young woman, was raped and killed by the Police on the pretext of giving her a lift in a police vehicle at Dinajpur. Sheema was raped and killed in the Police lockup at Chittagong. Tania, a girl aged 4, was violated in the Police control room of CMM Court at Dhaka. Jalal, a Police informer, ended up in the overhead water tank at the DB office Dhaka. Many more unfortunate victims fall prey to the predators in Khaki Uniform supposed to protect the victim of crimes and maintain law and order. And this is the Police force entrusted to implement the PSA and to choose whether to prosecute someone under the PSA or under the Penal Code alleged to have committed the identical offence. In the result the obvious has happened. Crimes are on the increase. The PSA has become counter-productive. PSA in the hands, of the Police force that we have, is nothing but a lethal and deadly weapon in the hands of an overindulgent, frolicsome, mischievous, whimsical and capriciously unscrupulous and wicked child. The weapon and the child are equally baneful and dangerous. This wicked child must be taken to task by using the State Power and the weapon (the PSA) dumped so deep under the earth that it can never be retrieved. The combined and cumulative harm and mischief done by the so-called "seven star" and "five star" group of Mastans are far less than the harm and mischief done by the Police. They are the largest and most organised' group of gangsters and terrorists with licence to carry arms anywhere at any time.

136. In the backdrop of the facts and circumstances, the detailed discussions after the prolonged and elaborate deliberations of the learned Counsel for the petitioners and the learned Attorney-General, the decisions and the constitutional authorities cited by them and urging the court to take judicial notice of the law and order situation obtaining in the country we have been catapulted on to a high and delicate state to umpire a constitutional battle fought with the articulation, erudition, excellence and brilliance by both sides like the celebrated and immortal actors of the Shakespearean drama such as Sir Garrick, Sir Lawrence Olivier and Sir Alec Guiness. Many a dialogues having been uttered, speeches made, questions posed and answered and the decision and declaration sought for (and opposed) that the PSA be declared unconstitutional and void, I hear a distant voice in the form of a soliloquy asking questions and giving replies in the following forms:

(i) Was not the PSA a non Money Bill in terms of Article 81(1) of the Constitution?

(ii) Was it passed by the legislature as a Money Bill?

(iii) Did not the Parliament lack the competence to pass it as a Money Bill?

(iv) Did not the Speaker certify the Bill as a Money Bill under Article 81(3) of the Constitution in violation of Article 81(1) and in derogation of the power granted to him under Article 7(1) of the Constitution?

(v) Is not the immunity of a Bill as a Proceeding in Parliament from Judicial review under Article 78(1) of the Constitution lost, the moment it transgresses any provision of the Constitution?

(vi) Was the certificate given by the Speaker that the PSA was a Money Bill and hence conclusive for all purposes and cannot be questioned in court in the face of the condition imposed and criterion prescribed under Article 81(3) and 81(1)(a) to (f) respectively.

(vii) Did not the Bill and the certificate given by the Speaker overstep and transgress certain provision of the Constitution?

(viii) Are not the constitutional prerogative of the Hon'ble President under Article 80(3) inviolable and is not the Speaker barred from taking away the said Presidential Prerogative while certifying a non-Money Bill as a Money Bill?

(ix) Does not the PSA lack the minimal guidelines?

(x) Has not the PSA ousted the jurisdiction of the Court?

(xi) Are not the provisions of the PSA overlapping with those of the Penal Code?

Answers to all the above questions except No. VI are "yes", though in accordance with the dictates of the Constitution the answers ought to have been "no" and in respect of question No. VI "yes". I, thus, find no alternative but to pronounce and declare the PSA to be ultra vires the Constitution. The stench of this still-born child has fouled the democratic air so much so that the sooner it is buried the better.

137. In the result the Rules are made absolute. Let (জননিরাপত্তা বিশেষ বিধান) আইন 2000 the Public Safety (Special Provision) Act 2000 (Act No. 7 of 2000) be taken off the Statute Book forthwith.

There will be no order as to cost.

141. For avoiding repetition of facts I shall discuss the facts of Writ Petition No. 76 of 2001 and 4430 of 2000 and the principle of law followed in all other cases and subsequently huge number of writ petitions filed challenging the vires of the Jana Nirapatta (Bishesh Bidhan) Ain, 2000 hereinafter called the Act.

142. In Writ Petition No. 76 of 2001, (Monjur Morshed Khan and another vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and others) the petitioners challenged the vires of the Act on the grounds that the provisions of Public Safety Act, in particular section 10 thereof, being inherently prone to arbitrary and discriminatory application are therefore unconstitutional and void as being violative under the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 32 and 35 of the Constitution and arbitrary and discriminatory action relating to first information report lodged by Mr Abedur Rahman, on 26-12-2000 in Kulshi PS Chittagong initially being treated as under the provisions of the Penal Code and subsequently altered arbitrarily to one under section 10 of the Public Safety Act.

143. The short fact of the case is that the petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 were in Chittagong, attending the kulkhwani of younger brother of petitioner No. 1. Petitioner No. 2 accompanied by his wife went to purchase iftar items from the shop of respondent No. 5 on 26-12-2000 at about 4-00 PM and while he was returning home by their car, a number of mastans surrounded the car and began to obstruct respondent No. 2 and the driver of the vehicle. Petitioner No. 2 informed his father, Petitioner No. 1, over mobile telephone, narrated the occurrence to him and the fact that the car was obstructed by the miscreants/mastans and that there was a fear of further violence. Petitioner No. 1 in response to the phone call, came to the shop, and accompanied the petitioner No. 2 and returned back home.

144. The petitioners sent their men to Kulshi police station in the night to lodge First Information Report. On reaching the police station they came to know that first information report had been lodged by the respondent No. 5 alleging that the petitioner and some other unknown persons had hurled abuses at the respondent No. 5, torn his shirt, knocked down some of the iftar items in the shop and that some un-named persons had removed money from cash box. Respondent No. 4 registered Kulshi PS Case No. 15, dated 26-12-2001 under sections 143/448/223/420 and 380 of the Penal Code.

145. In the morning of 27-12-2000 the petitioners were informed that a carbon copy of the first information report on identical allegations, was now shown to be registered as Case No. 15, dated 26-12-2000, but the provisions of the Penal Code earlier mentioned had been substituted to treat the offence involved as being under section 10 of the PSA Apparently at the direction of the higher authorities, the substitution in the first information report was made in a grossly discriminatory manner, to victimise the petitioner No. 1 who is a prominent member of the leading opposition political party, BNP and his son, petitioner No. 2. first information report in relation to the assault on the petitioner No. 2 and his driver had been left in Khulshi police station by Mr Wahidul Alam but no case having been registered thereon. Md Mizanur Rahman, the Driver, filed a petition of complaint in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong on 31-12-2000 upon which the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate passed an order directing the Officer-in-Charge, Khulshi Police-Station, Chittagong to treat the petition as first information report, and to take necessary action.

146. Respondent No. 5, being the informant of the case, filed petition dated 27-12-2000 to the Officer-in-Charge, Khulshi Police-Station praying that he may withdraw the first information report dated 26-12-2000 which he had been induced to lodge on the basis of wrong allegation and categorically stating that the petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 were not involved.

147. The petitioners moved the Vacation Judge of the High Court Division for anticipatory bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2001. This Hon'ble Court directed the police not to disturb the petitioners and not to arrest them in connection with the Khulshi PS Case No. 15, dated 16-12-2000 pending in the court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong till one week after the vacation.

148. They challenged the Act on the ground that the Act itself is inherently an instrument of arbitrary power, and discriminatory and is violative of fundamental rights of citizens guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 32 and 35 of the Constitution and therefore, unconstitutional and void and that the Act allows the respondents and other prosecuting agencies to use it as an instrument to oppress the citizens as it has sought to do in the case of the petitioner for political victimisation and/or extortion, the violation of the petitioners' fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, particularly Articles 27, 31, 32 and 35 thereon and that the PSA does not contain any provision which states that it overrides other laws and that the prosecuting agencies are conferred with the unfettered power of 'pick and choose', conflicting with the fundamental part of the Constitution as between the persons alleged to have been committed offences which falls both within the definition of the offence under the Penal Code and under the Act and the provisions of the Act are more harsh, including denial of bail and to the procedural safeguards for a fair trial and to more severe punishments and that there is no guideline in the Act which provides the rational and objective basis for a choice to be made as to whether to proceed under the Act or under the Penal Code. For this reason the Act is unconstitutional and void as being ex facie violative of fundamental rights of the petitioners guaranteed by Articles 27, 31, 32 and 35 of the Constitution.

149. That a subsequent alteration by respondent No. 4 acting under the direction of respondent No. 2 and/or respondent No. 3 treating the offence alleged to be under the Penal Code to be offence under the Act constitutes malafide, arbitrary and discriminatory action which is violative of the fundamental rights of the petitioners. The petitioners have taken grounds in the writ petition mainly on the above facts that the PSA as being violative of the fundamental rights of the petitioners guaranteed by Articles 27, 31, 32 and 35 of the Constitution should be declared void. On the above terms Rule Nisi was issued by this court.

150. During hearing some supplementary affidavits were filed. In one of the supplementary affidavits, the petitioners stated some facts and craved leave of the court to urge the grounds mentioned therein at the time of hearing that is the processes in which the Parliament passed the bill as money bill and stated that after receiving the President's recommendation to move the Public Safety Special Provision Bill, 2000 as it involved expenditure from public money, the bill was presented to the Parliament which passed the bill as an Act on 30th January, 2000. The Speaker sent it to the President on 31-1-2000 for his assent, under Article 80 of the Constitution certifying it to be a money bill under Article 81(3) of the Constitution. The President assented to it on 14th February, 2000. No sooner the bill was passed it came to be known that it was passed as a money bill and sent to the President with a certificate required for such a bill for his assent under Article 80 of the Constitution.

151. Thereafter, some senior members of the Bar of the Supreme Court Bar Association submitted a written memorandum to the President where they maintained that the bill in question cannot be a money bill under Article 81 of the Constitution and in order to resolve all controversies the matter may be referred to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion under Article 106 of the Constitution.

152. It appears that for quite some time the press had reported statement and counter-statement of the President, Prime Minister and Speaker. Law Minister and the Home Minister. The President maintained that the bill which was presented to him for his re-commendation was a bill involving expenditure of Public money and not as a money bill. 153. The Speaker maintained that the Home Minister notified Parliament Secretariat on 27h January, 2000 to place before Parliament the bill as a money bill, for which the President's recommendation has been obtained. On passing of the bill as the money bill, the Speaker gave his certificate.

154. The Home Minister also expressed surprise as to how the President could say that it was not a money bill. 155. The office of the President issued a press release in which this was denied.

156. By reasons of the statements made herein above it was submitted that the Parliament passed the bill as a money bill when it was not competent to do so and the Speaker certifying it as a money bill under Article 81(3) has committed fraud on the Constitution and thereby acted in contravention of the provisions of the Constitution and the laws together with the certificate of the Speaker are void being incompetent and inconsistent with the Constitution and, in any view of the matter, it is void under Article 7 of the Constitution. Such a legislation lacking legislative competence and constituting fraud on the Constitution is also void being colorable exercise of legislative power inconsistent with the expressed provision of power of the Constitution.

157. By a further supplementary affidavit the petitioners annexed the charge-sheet being charge-sheet No. 4 dated 8-2-2001 under section 10 of the Public Safety Act submitted by the Police after due investigation which is Annexure-.X(3)..

By another supplementary Affidavit the petitioners annexed a certified copy of the order-sheet of Writ Petition No. 1593 of 1988 dated 30-10-88 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court, issuing Rule Nisi calling .upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned sections 2(f)(iv) to (viii) and (g), 16 and 17(c) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 should not be declared ultra vires of Article 39 of the Constitution and, as such, void and the proceeding in Special Tribunal Case No. 370 of 1988 and continuance thereof against the petitioners should not be declared to be without lawful authority.
